item.content:encoded:
The final week of the 2026 regular season has arrived and there is still much to be determined.
While six teams have clinched playoff spots and a few others are close, multiple playoff positions are still up for grabs. And from an individual perspective, there are awards that could be determined in the coming days.
Here’s what is at stake in the final week of the season.
Who will win the AL West and Central?
There’s no telling who will win these two divisions in the American League. The Rays have just about wrapped up the AL East, but the White Sox and Guardians are still battling for the AL Central, while the Rangers and Astros are battling for the West.
This is where things stand. The Rangers lead the Astros by one game in the AL West but Houston won the pivotal tiebreaker against Texas. That means if the two clubs end the season with the same record, the division would go to the Astros.
In the AL Central, the Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox, but Chicago holds the tiebreaker advantage. Any tie between the two clubs means the White Sox would win the division.
Who gets the last AL Wild Card spot?
The AL West and Central battles are directly linked to what’s happening for the final Wild Card spot. It’s very likely that one of those four aforementioned teams will grab the last AL Wild Card spot, unless the Blue Jays have something to say about it. Right now, the White Sox have a fairly comfortable three-game lead over the Blue Jays and Astros.
Could Yordan still win the Triple Crown?
For a while, Yordan Alvarez looked like he might win the MLB Triple Crown, leading the Majors in average, home runs and RBIs. Now, the lefty slugger and presumptive AL MVP winner might merely finish first or second in average, home runs and RBIs. Heading into the final week, Alvarez has a slight edge in average (.313) over Chandler Simpson (.309) and is second in home runs (40) behind Junior Caminero (41) and second in RBIs (99) behind Pete Alonso (105). Alvarez could still snag the AL Triple Crown, but it’ll take a monstrous final week.
Simpson’s unique season and quest for an unusual batting title
Back to Simpson for a second, though. The Rays outfielder is having an excellent season, hitting for average, swiping bases and playing solid outfield defense. What he hasn’t done, though, is hit a single home run. The last hitter to win a batting title without hitting a home run was Rod Carew in 1972. Even if he doesn’t win, he could be the first qualified hitter to bat .300 without a home run since Luis Castillo in 1999.
Will Misiorowski win the ERA title?
It's been a remarkable season for Jacob Misiorowski, who has a 1.86 ERA and 247 strikeouts after Sunday's outing against the Orioles. Assuming he's in line for one more start next weekend -- even if it's abbreviated like his three-inning outing on Sunday -- Misiorowski is in line to join some impressive company. If he can hold his ERA edge over Cam Schlittler's 1.94 mark, he'd join 2021 Corbin Burnes (2.43 ERA in 2021) as the only Brewers to win an ERA title.
If Misiorowski keeps his ERA under two and gets to 250 strikeouts, there's some other fun company he'll join. He'd be just the 13th pitcher (15th instance) since earned runs became official in 1913 to finish a season with a sub-2 ERA and 250-plus strikeouts. The last to do so was Jacob deGrom in 2018.
Will Schwarber or PCA lead the Majors in home runs?
Kyle Schwarber led the National League with 56 home runs last year. As hard as it is to believe, though, Schwarber has never led the Majors in home runs. That could change this year, as the Phillies’ slugger is tied for the MLB lead with 45 homers. The last Phillie to pull that off was Ryan Howard in 2008, when he hit 48 homers and helped lead Philly to a World Series title.
Schwarber, though, has Pete Crow-Armstrong tied with him at the top. The surefire NL MVP has completely taken off this season with 45 homers, 38 stolen bases (more on this shortly), a .949 OPS and his usual excellent center field defense, which has led to an MLB-best 10.5 WAR, per FanGraphs. If PCA surpasses Schwarber, he’d be the first Cub to lead the NL in homers since Sammy Sosa’s 49 homers in 2002 and the first to lead the Majors in long balls since Sosa hit 50 in 2000.
Does PCA get to 40-40?
Crow-Armstrong is making all sorts of history this season. Reaching 10 WAR puts PCA in rarified territory and it seems very likely that the Cubs’ superstar center fielder will be a unanimous MVP winner, something no Cub has ever achieved. Crow-Armstrong is also a mere two stolen bases away from a 40-40 season, something no Cub has done and only six other MLB players have achieved.
Burleson vying to join impressive Cardinals history
Alec Burleson leads the Majors with 111 RBIs, putting him in line for some impressive Cardinals history. He’s looking to become the first Cardinal to lead the National League since Albert Pujols in 2010 and the first to lead the Majors in the category since Joe Torre drove in 137 runs in 1971. His stiffest competition is Cincinnati’s Sal Stewart, who sits at 110 RBIs entering the final week.
How does Verlander's final start go?
Justin Verlander returned to the Tigers for the 2026 season, which will be his final before retiring. Unfortunately, he only made one start in April and hasn't pitched since that point. The good news is he's lined up to pitch on Saturday at Detroit's Comerica Park, which will surely be a feel good moment and send off for the likely future Hall of Famer. Verlander can also add a few more strikeouts to his career total of 3,554.

item.content:encoded:
There’s a lot on the line before the 2026 regular season wraps up on Sunday, including postseason seeding, statistical milestones and player development. And even for the players and teams who won’t be chasing a World Series title, finishing the season strong is always important.
With the help of MLB.com’s beat writers, here is one player to watch on each team during the final week of the regular season.
American League East
Blue Jays: 1B Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
Over and over again, the flashes we’ve seen from Guerrero have fizzled. He was the face of the Blue Jays’ run to Game 7 of the World Series a year ago, but now, he’s the face of their disappointing 2026. It’s still so easy to believe in Guerrero when you see these flashes of his incredible talent, but he’s hit just nine home runs this season and has been living with an OPS under .700, stunning numbers for someone of his stature. Still, he’s the player with the most power to change this team’s trajectory, and if anyone can help salvage this season, it’s Guerrero. -- Keegan Matheson
Orioles: 1B Pete Alonso
Who else? If the O’s are going to make an improbable push into the postseason as a Wild Card team, it will likely be because of Alonso, who has done everything in his power to keep his team in the race down the stretch. There have been only nine 40-plus-homer seasons in Orioles history (since 1954), but Alonso could join the list with a strong finish to his first campaign in Baltimore. -- Jake Rill
Rays: 3B Junior Caminero
With all due respect to Chandler Simpson’s bid for both the AL batting crown and stolen-base title, this one’s pretty simple. Caminero has established himself as a legitimate candidate for the AL MVP Award alongside Yordan Alvarez. He’s leading the AL in home runs. He’s tracking toward starting all 162 games at third base. He’s the best player on the best team in the AL. And as an opening act for his first real moment in the postseason spotlight, he hit the first two walk-off homers of his career -- including one to clinch a playoff berth. Caminero’s power and energy always make him a player to watch, and that’s especially true as the Rays work to lock down their first division title since 2021. -- Adam Berry
Red Sox: LHP Garrett Crochet
The ace lefty is in a race against time to help the Red Sox as a reliever by the Wild Card round of the playoffs. Here is what's on the docket for Crochet: at least one live batting practice session at Fenway Park early in the week. After that, he would likely throw another live BP or a simulated game. An outside possibility would be the Red Sox getting him a tune-up in a regular-season game. Crochet last pitched for the Sox on April 25 before going down with a left shoulder injury. Most players wouldn’t go cold turkey into the playoffs after not pitching for so long, but Crochet has the chance to make the type of impact that could make it worthwhile. -- Ian Browne
Yankees: RHP Cam Schlittler
No matter where you stand on the issue of a pitcher winning the MVP Award, there’s no debating that Schlittler has earned that title within the Yankees’ clubhouse, putting the finishing touches on the club’s best pitching season since Ron Guidry in 1978. Those Yankees won a championship, and now the current group will lean on the 25-year-old from Walpole, Mass., to lead them toward the Canyon of Heroes for the first time since 2009. -- Bryan Hoch
AL Central
Guardians: 3B José Ramírez
Ramírez has produced below his superstar standard this season, in which he has dealt with the aftereffects of left hamate surgery he underwent in June. It’s something he’ll have to manage the remainder of 2026, but the 34-year-old might be turning it on at the right time. Ramírez is 8-for-17 with three doubles, one home run and three RBIs in his past four games. -- Tim Stebbins
Royals: C Carter Jensen
Jensen’s breakout rookie season has cemented him alongside Bobby Witt Jr. and Jac Caglianone as a core piece for a club looking to compete again in 2027. He’s already set Royals rookie records for home runs (25) and extra-base hits (60). Oh, and he’s done it while batting leadoff (he holds another record there, too) and taking over everyday catching duties from Salvador Perez. -- Jackson Stone
Tigers: SS/3B Kevin McGonigle
This could be the week that McGonigle wraps up the AL Rookie of the Year race. He’s the first rookie since Aaron Judge in 2017, and the fifth since 1990, to reach base safely 256 times in a season. He has more walks (94) than strikeouts (92) and is just the fifth rookie in the Divisional Era (since 1969) with that many walks in a season. And he joins Ted Williams as the only rookies in history to post at least 95 runs, 26 doubles, 17 homers, 70 RBIs and 93 walks. He has a chance to lead all AL position players in Baseball-Reference WAR, entering Sunday atop the AL at 6.8. -- Jason Beck
Twins: OF Emmanuel Rodriguez
Rodriguez has already shown his all-around skill set, from power to plate discipline to speed and defense. The only thing that has held him back over his pro career has been health, and now that he’s on the field, he’s hard to take your eyes off. Rodriguez is one of a slew of young Twins trying to cement their spots on the 2027 roster. -- Courtney Hollmon
White Sox: 1B Munetaka Murakami
Right-handed reliever Mike Vasil, also known as the Windy City Wizard for his dugout wand magic, said it best about Murakami: When he goes, the team goes. Murakami changed this franchise upon his arrival from Japan, taking the focus off a 6-13 team start and putting it upon his strong exploits on the field. Murakami has struggled since the start of August but showed his importance via a mammoth three-run home run in the first inning of a 3-1 victory over Detroit on Thursday. If Murakami can get hot over these final two series, the White Sox could punch their unexpected playoff ticket. -- Scott Merkin
AL West
Angels: C/1B/DH Moisés Ballesteros
Ballesteros got off to a slow start after being acquired in a trade that sent reliever Ryan Zeferjahn to the Cubs at the Trade Deadline but has been heating up offensively in September. He’s also been faring better than expected defensively at both catcher and first base. The 22-year-old was ranked as a Top 100 prospect by MLB Pipeline before each of the last two seasons, and the Angels would love to see him develop into a much-needed power bat from the left side. -- Rhett Bollinger
Astros: DH Yordan Alvarez
Shortstop Jeremy Peña said it best Thursday: “Obviously, Yordan is our horse.” After a 35-game stretch (Aug. 3-Sept. 13) in which he slashed .242/.380/.383 with three homers (since Aug. 3) to loosen his grip on the AL MVP Award, Alvarez homered in two of three games against the Royals last week and is still in contention for the Triple Crown. Alvarez leads the AL in batting average (.313) and is second in homers (40) and RBIs (99). -- Brian McTaggart 
Athletics: OF Henry Bolte
The A’s saw a five-tool talent in Bolte when they drafted him out of high school in 2022, and that has played out this year as he’s become just the third rookie in franchise history with at least 10 home runs and 20 stolen bases in a season and the first since Mitchell Page in 1977. Still just scratching the surface of his abilities, Bolte is building for what could be true star potential from him in 2027. -- Martín Gallegos
Mariners: INF/OF Michael Arroyo
Seattle's No. 3 prospect and MLB Pipeline's No. 42 overall prospect has played sparingly -- just five starts in the team’s 13 games since he made his MLB debut on Sept. 6. But that's been primarily due to a lack of positional runway. He came up as a second baseman but has transitioned more to left field this season. However, both those spots are occupied (by Cole Young and Randy Arozarena, respectively). Arroyo is a big part of the club's longer-term plans and has shown what he can do with the bat. How he's used in this final week could be a springboard for 2027. -- Daniel Kramer
Rangers: SS Corey Seager
Seager is the engine that keeps the Rangers offense going, and his absence has been felt throughout his three separate stints on the injured list this season (twice with back issues, once with a concussion). As he played sporadically in the first half, Seager hit just .182/.292/.374 as he battled injuries. Since returning from his last IL stint on July 31, he’s hitting .285 with an .837 OPS and eight homers in 45 games. The Rangers will only go as far as Seager takes them. And lately, he looks like the player who can put the team on his back. -- Kennedi Landry
National League East
Braves: RHP Robert Suarez
Suarez made a rehab appearance on Sunday with Triple-A Gwinnett, striking out one in a scoreless inning. The veteran reliever hasn’t pitched in the Majors since he was shut down in late June with a 0.56 ERA. There’s hope he will pitch in a big league game before the postseason begins, but the Braves haven’t committed to activating him before the regular season concludes. -- Mark Bowman
Marlins: SS Otto Lopez
A 2026 All-Star, Lopez needs 15 hits over his final six games to become the first Marlin since Luis Arraez in 2023 to reach 200 hits. Lopez (.305) trails Arraez (.313) and D-backs catcher Gabriel Moreno (.307) for the National League batting title. If Lopez can somehow leapfrog that pair, he would be the fourth NL batting champion in franchise history, joining Arraez ('23), Dee Strange-Gordon ('15) and Hanley Ramirez ('09). -- Christina De Nicola
Mets: RHP Jonah Tong
Few Mets players have as much to prove as Tong, who spent most of this season in the Minors before recently returning and flashing some much-improved form. If Tong can finish the year with another solid start, he will position himself well for what’s sure to be a lively rotation competition next spring. If he falters, he’ll only give the Mets more reason to be wary of him. -- Anthony DiComo
Nationals: OF James Wood
Wood slugged his way into his second All-Star selection, then missed 27 games because of a left oblique strain. He returned from the IL on Sept. 2 and is batting .259 with a .698 OPS this month. Wood, who just turned 24 on Thursday, will look to make up for the time he lost to injury and close out the final week of the season strong. -- Jessica Camerato
Phillies: LHP Jesús Luzardo
Luzardo is on the 15-day injured list with inflammation in his left shoulder. He’s eligible to be activated on Sunday, the final game of the regular season. It doesn’t necessarily matter if he pitches or not that day. It matters if the Phillies think Luzardo, who began throwing on Sunday, can pitch in the NL Wild Card Series, which begins on Sept. 29. If he can pitch, can he start? Or does he come out of the bullpen? He’s been arguably baseball’s best pitcher for months, so the Phillies need him one way or another. -- Todd Zolecki
NL Central
Brewers: RHP Jacob Misiorowski
Misiorowski probably has the National League Cy Young Award locked up. And his final regular-season start later this week will probably be tapered, since there’s no need to push his pitch count into dangerous territory. But the outing is still important, because it offers the Brewers’ young ace one final opportunity to build confidence going into what will surely be a Game 1 start in the NL Division Series. No club better showcases the fact that baseball is a team sport, but there’s little doubt that Misiorowski is singularly important to Milwaukee’s October hopes. -- Adam McCalvy
Cardinals: 1B Alec Burleson
Outfielder Jordan Walker received a lot of publicity because of his breakout season and winning the T-Mobile Home Run Derby, but Burleson is the man on the Cardinals, currently leading the Major Leagues with 111 RBIs. The last Cardinal to lead the big leagues in that department was Joe Torre (137) in 1971, and the last to lead the National League was Albert Pujols (118) in 2010. Burleson also leads the Majors with 61 hits with runners in scoring position, the most by a Cardinal since Brian Jordan (62) in 1996. -- Bill Ladson
Cubs: OF Pete Crow-Armstrong
All the “P-C-A” chants at Wrigley Field have transformed into “M-V-P” chants every time Crow-Armstrong steps to the plate for the North Siders. Crow-Armstrong is vying to become just the seventh player in MLB history to finish with at least 40 homers and 40 stolen bases. Beyond keeping an eye on how high he can get those numbers, Cubs fans want to see just how high Crow-Armstrong’s MLB-leading WAR (10.5, per FanGraphs) can get before season’s end. And then, of course, the question will be whether the star center fielder can play like an MVP in October. -- Jordan Bastian
Pirates: SS Konnor Griffin
Pittsburgh fans have received small samples of what Griffin can do as baseball’s former top prospect. After missing most of the summer due to two separate IL stints, Griffin has become a regular at shortstop and in the leadoff spot to finish out his rookie campaign. To put it simply, Griffin is both the present and the future. Keep a close eye on his continued ascension in the final week. -- Aiden Stepansky
Reds: 1B Sal Stewart
Stewart will be trying to put the finishing touches on a season that should net him the NL Rookie of the Year Award. The 22-year-old is the 14th rookie since 1920 to post a 30-homer, 100-RBI season, and each of the last nine that did it since the award started in 1947 have won it, the most recent being Pete Alonso for the Mets in 2019. Stewart is currently second in MLB overall in RBIs with 110. If he can overtake Burleson, he would be the third rookie to finish a season leading in that category since RBIs became an official statistic in 1913, joining Ted Williams (1939) and Walt Dropo (1950). -- Mark Sheldon
NL West
D-backs: OF Corbin Carroll
Carroll battled a lower back issue which clearly hampered him at the plate, but after taking a couple of days off to rest, he has begun to swing the bat much better. As the D-backs have seen many times in the past when Carroll gets hot, it’s something to see. If they get his bat going and Gabriel Moreno and Nolan Arenado continue to swing it the way they have, the D-backs will have a puncher’s chance during the final week. -- Steve Gilbert
Dodgers: TWP Shohei Ohtani
Ohtani landed on the 15-day IL for the first time as a Dodger when his ongoing right biceps and left knee issues lingered into the beginning of September. He is done for the season as a pitcher, but he's expected back as a hitter. The final week of the regular season will be important for Ohtani, whether he returns in time to play a few games or tunes up his swing behind the scenes. -- Sonja Chen
Giants: 1B Bryce Eldridge
Now that Rafael Devers is out for the season, Eldridge -- once he clears concussion protocol --  has the chance to play first base every day for the Giants. The 21-year-old rookie has made some impressive strides with his defense, but his calling card remains his big bat, which has produced several majestic homers this year, including a 461-foot blast on Tuesday night at Busch Stadium. The Giants have struggled to develop star hitters in recent years, but Eldridge’s tantalizing power should give them plenty to dream on heading into 2027. -- Maria Guardado
Padres: RHP Nick Pivetta
Pivetta missed nearly five months with a flexor strain in his right elbow. His first few starts since returning have been mostly solid. The Padres have serious rotation questions heading into the postseason and will be assessing Pivetta’s final outing with a keen eye on what kind of usage might lie ahead for him in October. If they can get the dominant version of Pivetta that finished sixth in NL Cy Young voting last season, it would go a long way. -- AJ Cassavell
Rockies: 1B TJ Rumfield
Blocked in the Yankees organization, Rumfield flourished after being acquired in a quiet deal last offseason. His stingy at-bats -- with the patience to draw a walk, fight off tough pitches and shorten up and go the other way -- are examples of the offensive culture shift the Rockies are seeking. There is power potential. He has hit home runs in spurts this year, and a year's experience -- not just on the field, but dealing with the grind of a Major League season -- could lead to even more pop. -- Thomas Harding

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Why Cam Schlittler was pissed at himself after NY's loss to Diamondbacks appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Cam Schlittler wasn't happy with his performance on the mound after the New York Yankees' 5-3 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday night.
Schlittler is going through the second season of his career in the majors with the Yankees. He has quickly broken out as one of the best young pitchers, helping New York be firm in the playoff picture this year.
Schlittler started on the mound as he lasted six innings, striking out six batters while conceding three hits and one earned run. New York lost on Pavin Smith's pinch-hit, two-run homer in the ninth inning, resulting in Arizona's victory. He blamed himself for those mistakes after the game.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"I mean, I wouldn't say I really gave them a chance,'' Schlittler said. "That one's kind of on me, so I'll take the blame for that. Made an error there, let up two runs."
"I mean, there's still a chance,'' Schlittler said, "but we got to play our (butts) off a little bit.'
How Cam Schlittler, Yankees played against Diamondbacks
Cam Schlittler and the Yankees have preparation for the postseason. These last games of the regular season will decide their place in the AL bracket, needing every win they can get.
The game was scoreless throughout the first four innings, seeing both teams finally get on the board in the fifth frame. However, Arizona dealt more blows as New York was unable to muster up more big plays to rally back against the hosts.
New York fell to an 89-65 record on the season, sitting at second place in the AL East Division standings. They are above the Boston Red Sox and the Toronto Blue Jays while trailing the Tampa Bay Rays.
The Yankees will look to bounce back in their series finale against the Diamondbacks. That contest commences on Sept. 20 at 4:10 p.m. ET.
Related: Yankees' Spencer Jones shuts down injury concern ahead of postseason
Related: Yankees' Aaron Judge breaks silence after returning to IL

item.title: [tsn.ca] Rangers put pitcher Quantrill on IL due to right lat tightness
item.dc:creator: ESPN Staff

Hard-throwing right-hander Winston Santos was recalled from Triple-A Round Rock and joined the Rangers before the finale of their three-game series against the Toronto Blue Jays. item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- The American League West-leading Texas Rangers put versatile right-hander Cal Quantrill on the 15-day injured list Sunday, a day after he exited following four batters and 12 pitches because of right lat tightness.
Hard-throwing right-hander Winston Santos was recalled from Triple-A Round Rock and joined the Rangers before the finale of their three-game series against the Toronto Blue Jays.
About an hour before the game, the Rangers said right fielder Brandon Nimmo was being scratched from the starting lineup because of illness.
Before the IL move was announced, manager Skip Schumaker said the Rangers knew going into Saturday night’s game that Quantrill’s velocity was lower.
Quantrill (9-5) was showing no signs of pain when Schumaker, pitching coach Jordan Tiegs and head trainer Matt Lucero went to the mound in the second inning and he came out of the game. Quantrill has a 2.86 ERA in 32 games (15 starts) after going to spring training with the Rangers on a minor league deal.
He left his previous start after six innings and 70 pitches at Arizona last Sunday with back soreness.
Quantrill, 31, has a 1.75 ERA (11 earned runs in 56⅔ innings) over his past 11 appearances (10 starts). Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees at 1.64 is the only qualified pitcher with a better ERA over that span.
Santos is beginning his third stint with the Rangers, though his only appearance in the first two was his big league debut July 1 at Cleveland, where he allowed two runs in two innings. He has 103 strikeouts in 83⅓ innings in the minor leagues this season.

item.title: [bleedcubbieblue.com] 2026 Cubs Heroes and Goats: Michael Busch is the Superhero vs. the Reds
item.dc:creator: Thomas Smith
item.description: There just haven’t been enough games like Saturday’s for the Cubs this year. It wasn’t easy. It never is with this team if they aren’t scoring 10 plus runs. But the pitching was really good save for one rough inning in the fifth that probably wasn’t as bad as it looked, aided by a weird, bad throw from Dansby Swanson on a relay play. That led to one of the two runs that the Cubs did allow in this one to being unearned. Daniel Palencia followed and was terrific. Aaron Civale was a little shaky. R
item.content:encoded:
There just haven’t been enough games like Saturday’s for the Cubs this year. It wasn’t easy. It never is with this team if they aren’t scoring 10 plus runs. But the pitching was really good save for one rough inning in the fifth that probably wasn’t as bad as it looked, aided by a weird, bad throw from Dansby Swanson on a relay play. That led to one of the two runs that the Cubs did allow in this one to being unearned. Daniel Palencia followed and was terrific. Aaron Civale was a little shaky. Ryan Zeferjahn is really tough to watch despite clearly immense talent. I’ve not followed his career and haven’t dug into it, but without doing so, I can confidently say that every coach he’s ever has dreamed of a fully unlocked Zeferjahn who might be a truly elite pitcher. Ryan Rolison faced one batter, doing his job and recording a save.
Fun fact, this team has allowed exactly two runs 34 times this year. They are 26-8 (.765) when they do so. I was surprised it was so many games, given the struggles of this pitching staff. They’ve allowed two or fewer 50 times. They have a record of 42-8 in those games. If you mentally shed a tear for this team not having a healthy dose of 2024 Justin Steele, 2025 Cade Horton or 2026 Ben Brown, this is why. I heard it said on the Marquee pregame Saturday that this position player group should have led to a 100-plus win team. It felt so bold. But it’s totally true. With reasonable pitching, this is a 100-plus win team. And that’s why the postseason is not completely hopeless. If they get some pitching, they can win.
On the other side of the ball, the Cubs turned eight hits and three walks and a hit batter into five runs. So slightly less traffic than the night before, but one more run. Two homers and not one. A double to go with it. But more than anything, it was just clustering things together a little better. For the second straight night, the Cubs got largely nothing out of the duo of Pete Crow-Armstrong and Alex Bregman, who have led the way for this team, particularly in the second half. The rest of the lineup was pretty balanced and the offense was a team effort.
It’s been a week now since the last double-digit offensive game. It’s probably not worth a lot of mention, but it seems like the Cubs get one of those every week or 10 days. So that’s probably coming somewhere in the near term. It would be nice to get one of those easier ones and not to have to sweat every inning as this team closes in on clinching a playoff spot and tries to secure the top Wild Card. Regardless, the Cubs will have a chance to win a third straight series on Sunday afternoon and that’s what you want to see. It’s been a welcome bounceback after the nightmare in Milwaukee. As I said following that last game there, this team is very professional. They’ll bounce back and this won’t linger. It was a really good time to be right.
With any luck, this team will just keep on winning series as the season winds down. Win Sunday afternoon, get home and take a series from a Marlins team that is fighting down to the wire despite being eliminated. The Marlins are in San Diego and we’ll catch them coming back east after playing there and in Arizona. That’s a tough trip. Especially when the clock strikes midnight on your season mid trip. Nine-game trips are always hard. But three good teams, a couple of different time zones (that are both different from their home time zone), different styles of play. It’s a lot. Then the Cubs get a Red Sox team that is pretty squarely locked into the second Wild Card spot. They’ll want to be lining up pitching for their Wild Card series which very likely will be against the Yankees. Of course, the Cubs will be getting theirs set too. But the gap between one and six for Cub starters just isn’t massive (which is damning with faint praise).
Anyway, it was a good night in Cincinnati. Seiya Suzuki seems to be coming out of a slump a little bit. Three singles in the last two games. Only one really hit hard, but using the field and having some success. Michael Busch hit a monster homer. Dansby Swanson had his rehab washed out, but save for the weird throw, he looked like he’s ready to contribute. He had a single and a homer of his own. Good to get Dansby back. It’s his defense that provides most of his value. But, Dansby has the mind and approach of a superstar. He doesn’t shy from the biggest moments. That’s not a bad bat to have down at eight or nine in your lineup. This team is better with Dansby on the field. Just as it usually is with Ian Happ on the field. A player need not be a Superstar to produce consistent positive value for a team.
Three Positives:
- Daniel Palencia faced six batters in the sixth and seventh inning. That sixth inning was huge with just a one-run lead and the 2-3-4 hitters due up for the Reds. He was fairly efficient and got a second inning of work. He’s looked better the last couple of times and is maybe re-finding himself just in time.
- Dansby Swanson had a single and a homer, scored twice.
- Michael Busch had a single, a homer and was hit by a pitch. He scored once. He had a really nice homestand before this trip (.316/.417/.526). He hasn’t really hit a groove all year long. Maybe he too is hitting his peak at just the right time?
Game 155, September 19: Cubs 5, Reds 2 (86-69)
Reminder: Heroes and Goats are determined by WPA scores and are in no way subjective.
THREE HEROES:
- Superhero: Michael Busch (.208). 2-3, HR, HBP, RBI, R
- Hero: Daniel Palencia (.197). 2 IP, 6 BF, 3K
- Sidekick: Seiya Suzuki (.128). 2-3, BB, RBI
THREE GOATS:
- Billy Goat: Tyrone Taylor (-.125). 0-3
- Goat: Carson Kelly (-.094). 0-4
- Kid: Pete Crow-Armstrong (-.082). 0-5
WPA Play of the Game: Michael Busch hit a solo homer with one out in the sixth to give the Cubs a one run lead. (.167)
Reds Play of the Game: JJ Bleday singled with a runner on first and one outs, the Reds down two in the fifth. This is the play where Dansby Swanson threw it past Alex Bregman at third, allowing a run to score. (.149)
Cubs Player of the Game:
Game 154 Winner: Carson Kelly received just 17 of 43 votes, but with very divided voting, that was enough to win.
Rizzo Award Standings: (Top 5/Bottom 5)
The award is named for Anthony Rizzo, who finished first in this category three of the first four years it was in existence and four times overall. He also recorded the highest season total ever at +65.5. The point scale is three points for a Superhero down to negative three points for a Billy Goat.
- Alex Bregman +25
- Pete Crow-Armstrong +22.5
- Carson Kelly +17.5
- Shōta Imanaga +15
- Ben Brown +13.5
- Jameson Taillon -13
- Nico Hoerner -16
- Dansby Swanson -17
- Seiya Suzuki -17
- Caleb Thielbar -17.5
Scoreboard Watching: The Phillies lost for the second straight night. They fall one game behind the Cubs, while the Padres won and are tied with the Cubs. The Cubs hold tiebreakers over both teams. The Diamondbacks won a game started by Cam Schlittler, finding some offense against him and then walking it off to win. The Arizona win delays the eventual Cub playoff clinch. That’s two this week as they try to keep their very narrow playoff hopes alive. Even with the win, they remain four games behind the Phillies for the last playoff spot.
Up Next: The Cubs finish the series with the Reds. David Peterson (8-8, 5.11) starts for the Cubs. David is 2-1 with a 4.31 over his last seven, including a win last time against the Braves, allowing a run on three hits and three walks over six innings. The general trend for Peterson is about four good starts to every bad one and they are very stratified. So once he gets it going, he usually delivers. Look to see if he can get locked in early in Cincy. Certainly a guy who likes to keep the ball down is a welcome choice in that park. He held the Reds to two runs over five at Wrigley at the end of August. But they also saw him twice as a Met and did quite well against him (nine runs in eight innings of work).
24-year-old Rhett Lowder (6-11, 5.79) has had a rough first full year as a starter (27 appearances, 24 starts). The strain of a long season may be weighing him down as the year draws towards a close. He’s 2-4 with a 7.13 over his last seven games. He’s allowed 45 hits and 12 walks in just 35.1 innings over those seven starts. The Cubs have seen him twice as a starter and once as a reliever. As a starter, he’s allowed six runs in just eight innings of work. The two relief innings were scoreless, though he issued two walks. He and Peterson faced each other in that game in August. Lowder won, despite allowing three runs over five innings. He did a good job that night staying in the strike zone, not walking anyone (the only time he’s done so since July). He hasn’t won since that start at the end of August, losing all three starts (Brewers, Dodgers, Dodgers, ouch).
Get the offense going early and see if you can post some crooked numbers and ride that to a win. Don’t let Lowder settle in and find some of what made him a 7th overall pick in 2023. He’ll probably eventually be a good starter. But how about not now?

item.title: [si.com] Cam Schlittler Enters MLB History With Sandy Koufax, Bob Gibson During Cy Young Race
item.dc:creator: Justin Binkowski; Unknown
item.description: New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler has joined two Hall of Fame pitchers in the record books after what was likely his second-to-last start of the 2026 regular season. Schlittler tossed six innings against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday, giving up one earned run on three hits and three walks while striking out six. item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees right-hander Cam Schlittler has joined two Hall of Fame pitchers in the record books after what was likely his second-to-last start of the 2026 regular season.
Schlittler tossed six innings against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Saturday, giving up one earned run on three hits and three walks while striking out six. This was the 24th time this season the right-hander hasn't allowed more than one earned run in a start, tying Hall of Famers Bob Gibson and Sandy Koufax for the second-most such starts since 1920, according to MLB.com's Sarah Langs. Koufax is also at the top of that list with 25 starts in which he gave up no more than one earned run, so the Yankees hurler will have a chance to tie the Dodgers legend again in his final regular-season outing of the year.
This stat is just the latest example of how truly dominant Schlittler has been this season. In fact, some fans have been debating whether the hard-throwing righty could be a legitimate contender for the 2026 American League MVP. At the very least, the young pitcher has made a strong case for the 2026 AL Cy Young Award.
Has Cam Schlittler already done enough to claim the AL Cy Young?
With just one week left in the 2026 MLB regular season, the two pitchers with the best chance to win the American League Cy Young Award are Schlittler and Toronto Blue Jays right-hander Dylan Cease. Schlittler now has an AL-leading 1.94 ERA in 32 starts this year, racking up 234 strikeouts in 190 2/3 innings. Meanwhile, Cease leads the American League with 239 strikeouts and has a 2.40 ERA in 169 innings.
In Cease's most recent start on Friday, the 30-year-old threw just 2 2/3 innings and walked six batters. He had an MRI done on his shoulder Saturday night and is no longer expected to make his next scheduled start on Wednesday, according to The Athletic's Mitch Bannon. While the Toronto hurler could pitch again later in the week, this may impact his chances of making a late push for the 2026 AL Cy Young Award.
As things stand, Schlittler seems like the frontrunner for this year's AL Cy Young Award. But the final week of the regular season could play a last-minute role in the eventual outcome.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.title: [MLB.com] ¿Qué les espera a los Yankees sin Judge en esta última semana?
item.dc:creator: David Venn

item.content:encoded:
Nueva York llegó al domingo a 5.0 juegos de la cima del Este de la Liga Americana, detrás de los encendidos Rays. Tampa Bay estuvo programado para concluir su serie en casa ante los Medias Rojas el domingo, al mismo tiempo que los Yankees se preparaban para hacer lo propio frente a los Diamondbacks en Arizona.
Luego, los Bombarderos del Bronx recibirán desde el martes al equipo de St. Petersburg en el Bronx para una crucial serie de cuatro juegos. Dicha serie podría apretar la lucha por el Este, o de una vez por todas ser decisiva para que los Rays terminen de ganar la llave y dejar a los Yankees como un Comodín. Después de eso, Nueva York concluirá su temporada regular con una serie de tres choques en casa frente a Baltimore.
Ahora, la gran interrogante para Nueva York es cómo jugará el equipo sin Judge en la alineación.
“Tengo confianza”, dijo el dirigente del equipo, Aaron Boone. “Obvio, quitar al mejor jugador lo hace más difícil. Pero creo que en las últimas semanas, hemos empezado a encontrar el ritmo un poco a nivel ofensivo”.
Es cierto. Aunque los Yankees llegaron al domingo en el lugar número 21 de Grandes Ligas en carreras anotadas después del Juego de Estrellas, en los últimos 30 días, han anotado la mayor cantidad de carreras en la Liga Americana, superados sólo por los fuertes equipos de Cerveceros y Cachorros en las Mayores. Y en ese trecho, están empatados en la cima del Joven Circuito con 37 jonrones… incluyendo uno solo de Judge, quien dio uno el lunes en Minnesota como parte de su trecho de siete partidos jugados entre su fractura en una costura sufrida al principio de la campaña y su lesión de ahora, un tirón en la pantorrilla derecha.
“Sabemos que somos capaces de ganar juegos”, expresó Boone. “Hemos tenido que jugar sin muchas piezas cruciales en diferentes momentos y durante largos trechos de la temporada, así que nuestra expectativa es salir y ganar. Y se acabó el tema”.
Otra declaración acertada. Dirigiendo un equipo que ha contado con apenas 24 juegos de Giancarlo Stanton, los Yankees – como la gran mayoría de los conjuntos – han sabido soportar lesiones de otras piezas clave. En estos momentos, esperan la llegada muy pronto de figuras como Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trent Grisham y posiblemente Ryan Weathers.
“Espero que más y más piezas puedan volver y hacer de este equipo uno más formidable el resto del camino”, dijo Boone.
Por supuesto, el punto fuerte de los Yankees del 2026 ha sido su pitcheo. Encabezados por el candidato al Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, Cam Schlittler, los Yankees son los líderes en MLB con efectividad colectiva de 3.18, 0.38 mejor que el segundo mejor equipo en ese sentido, los Cerveceros. Su rotación abridora es la mejor del béisbol, con promedio de carreras limpias de 3.25, a la vez que su bullpen está empatado con el de Boston en el primer puesto con 3.09.
Entonces, aunque la presencia de Judge representaría una gran mejoría para cualquier lineup del planeta, los Yankees han sabido sobrevivir sin él en sentido general desde el 31 de mayo. ¿Será ése el caso en una posible Serie de Comodín frente a los Medias Rojas la próxima semana si no vuelve “El Juez”?
“Espero que más y más piezas puedan volver y hacer de este equipo uno más formidable el resto del camino”, dijo Boone, sin mencionar específicamente a Judge en ese contexto.

Su rotación abridora es la mejor del béisbol, con promedio de carreras limpias de 3.25, a la vez que su bullpen está empatado con el de Boston en el primer puesto con 3.09.
Entonces, aunque la presencia de Judge representaría una gran mejoría para cualquier lineup del planeta, los Yankees han sabido sobrevivir sin él en sentido general desde el 31 de mayo. ¿Será ése el caso en una posible Serie de Comodín frente a los Medias Rojas la próxima semana si no vuelve “El Juez”?
Es una pregunta que nadie en el universo de los Yankees quiere ponderar en este momento.
“Esperamos tener el mejor resultado, pero todo depende de cómo irá el proceso de sanación”, manifestó Boone.

item.title: [bignewsnetwork.com] D-backs strive to make more 'magic' happen vs. Yankees
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.description: D-backs strive to make more 'magic' happen vs. Yankees (Photo credit: Matt Kartozian) Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said he felt 'a little bit of magic' in a 5-3 walk-off win over the New York Yankees on Saturday, the night the Diamondbacks celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series title. The Diamondbacks will take wins however they can get them as they continue an uphill fight for a National League wild-card berth in Sunday afternoon's finale of a three-game series vs. the Yank
item.content:encoded:
D-backs strive to make more 'magic' happen vs. Yankees
(Photo credit: Matt Kartozian)
Arizona manager Torey Lovullo said he felt 'a little bit of magic' in a 5-3 walk-off win over the New York Yankees on Saturday, the night the Diamondbacks celebrated the 25th anniversary of their 2001 World Series title.
The Diamondbacks will take wins however they can get them as they continue an uphill fight for a National League wild-card berth in Sunday afternoon's finale of a three-game series vs. the Yankees in Phoenix.
New York's Will Warren (10-6, 3.89 ERA) will oppose Arizona's Corbin Burnes (0-0, 5.87) in a battle of right-handers.
'There was a ton of energy in the stadium,' said Lovullo, noting that most of the players from the 2001 team were on hand, 'so maybe there was a little bit of magic somewhere in these rafters that everybody picked up on.'
Pavin Smith's two-run, game-winning homer saved the Diamondbacks for a night, but work remains.
'We have to get inside a certain number,' said Lovullo, whose team will finish the regular season next week with a pair of three-game series at Colorado and San Diego. 'We know it, and this team is driving for something they feel they are able to do.'
Arizona (81-74) is five games behind the Chicago Cubs (86-69) and San Diego (86-69) and four behind Philadelphia (85-70) for the NL's three wild-card spots. Each team has seven games remaining.
The Yankees (89-65) fell five games behind first-place Tampa Bay (94-60) in the AL East. Those teams will meet in a four-game series in Yankee Stadium beginning with a split doubleheader on Tuesday and already have clinched a postseason berth.
'I have a ton of confidence in the guys we have rolling out there right now,' New York manager Aaron Boone said after Aaron Judge (calf strain) landed on the 10-day injured list Saturday.
Warren worked the Yankees' playoff clincher Monday at Minnesota, although he did not get a decision after giving up two runs (both unearned) in 5 2/3 innings of an 8-3 win. He struck out six and walked two.
Warren has been a workhorse on a staff that has faced injury issues. He will make his 29th start, second on the team behind Cam Schlittler (32).
'We've got a veteran core that's been here before, and we're looking to do big things,' Warren said of the upcoming postseason.
Warren has faced the Diamondbacks once in his career, giving up two runs on one hit -- a Corbin Carroll two-run homer -- in five innings of a no-decision on April 1, 2025.
Burnes will make his third start since being activated from the injured list Sept. 8 after a 15-month absence following Tommy John surgery. He gave up five runs in 4 2/3 innings but didn't figure into the decision in Monday's 8-7 victory over Miami, striking out four with no walks.
'It's all about cutter command,' Burnes said of his pet pitch, which he traditionally throws about 50% of the time. 'Just have to be more consistent with that,'
Burnes is 0-2 with a 1.93 ERA in four career starts against the Yankees. Paul Goldschmidt is 10-for-34 with a homer against the four-time All-Star and 2021 NL Cy Young Award winner.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Cam Schlittler Joins Walter Johnson in Baseball History
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Cam Schlittler didn't earn a win on Saturday night, because the New York Yankees' bullpen let the game get away from them in Arizona against the Diamondbacks. Schlittler did, as he has done so often this season, make some more baseball history. This history requires us to go back more than a century to a man named Walter Johnson. Fans of baseball record books and history will know Johnson's name. He was known as the "Big Train," viewed by many as the first flamethrower that MLB ever had. Johnson
item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler didn't earn a win on Saturday night, because the New York Yankees' bullpen let the game get away from them in Arizona against the Diamondbacks.
Schlittler did, as he has done so often this season, make some more baseball history.
This history requires us to go back more than a century to a man named Walter Johnson.
Fans of baseball record books and history will know Johnson's name. He was known as the "Big Train," viewed by many as the first flamethrower that MLB ever had.
Johnson pitched for the Washington Senators, and he ranks second in the history of the sport in wins, behind just Cy Young.
He also, as one might expect, had some remarkable statistical feats during his day. And somehow, more than 100 years later, Schlittler has joined him on a couple lists.
Cam Schlittler and Walter Johnson
Schlittler's latest feat has to do with his ERA on the road, which has been finalized for the season because his last possible start will have to come at home in the week ahead.
The lanky righty has finished the year with a 1.16 ERA on the road.
The only player in the history of the American League to go lower than that is Johnson. In 1913, he had a 1.06 ERA on the road, according to New York Yankees Stats on X:
Cam Schlittler finishes the season with a 1.16 road ERA.
The only pitcher in American League history with a lower ERA on the road is Walter Johnson’s 1.06 in 1913 (min. 15 GS).
— New York Yankees Stats (@nyyankeesstats) September 20, 2026
Schlittler also is on a list for his entire body of work just behind Johnson. He's now got the third-most starts in a season in AL history in which he allowed no more than one earned run:
Most starts allowing 0-1 ER in a season, American League history (excluding openers)
27 Walter Johnson 1913
26 Walter Johnson 1914
24 Cam Schlittler 2026
— New York Yankees Stats (@nyyankeesstats) September 20, 2026
Baseball is such a cool sport historically, because all the information means that it's possible to realize that a pitcher in 2026 hasn't done something since a pitcher in 1913.
The game has obviously changed so much, but many of the numbers haven't, and it creates this great potential for comparison.
It also emphasizes just how special Schlittler has been this season. When you have to go back more than a century to find a peer, that's pretty incredible.
Cy Young Chatter
Schlittler is chasing the AL Cy Young, and a couple things have leaned in his favor this week.
For one, Dylan Cease had his worst outing of the season for the Toronto Blue Jays.
And as far as Cease is concerned, Toronto even has less of a chance to make the playoffs now, which lowers the overall vibes around his season relative to Schlittler.
It could still be close, but Schlittler is trying to put the finishing touches on his case for the award.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees' Cam Schlittler Joins Walter Johnson in Baseball History appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees news: Spencer Jones joins the walking wounded
item.dc:creator: Kevin Winterhalt
item.description: New York Post | Greg Joyce: The Yankees cannot afford any more additions to their M*A*S*H unit. Unfortunately, at least for Saturday, there is another. Spencer Jones, who’s been outstanding at the plate lately, was out of the starting lineup Saturday with a sore foot. For his part, Jones did not seem worried and attributed the soreness to playing in Arizona Friday after jamming his heel earlier in the week against the Twins. Here’s hoping he’s right. Yahoo Sports | Tate Mosher: Headed into what
item.content:encoded:
New York Post | Greg Joyce: The Yankees cannot afford any more additions to their M*A*S*H unit. Unfortunately, at least for Saturday, there is another. Spencer Jones, who’s been outstanding at the plate lately, was out of the starting lineup Saturday with a sore foot. For his part, Jones did not seem worried and attributed the soreness to playing in Arizona Friday after jamming his heel earlier in the week against the Twins. Here’s hoping he’s right.
Yahoo Sports | Tate Mosher: Headed into what was likely his penultimate regular season start of 2026, Cam Schlittler’s incredible campaign has the attention of people all over baseball. Cam’s been so sensational that he’s earned MVP chatter, an award that pitchers rarely hoist. The last to do it? Future Hall of Famer Clayton Kershaw. Earlier on Saturday, MLB’s official X account made sure everyone is tracking the similarities between the latter’s 2014 season and Cam’s 2026 campaign. Whether Schlittler can take home AL MVP or not, it’s been a heck of a ride. And you know you’ve had a brilliant season when you’re getting comped to Peak Kershaw.
MLB | Bryan Hoch: All Cam, all the time. The burgeoning ace has been so spectacular that it has become difficult for those closest to him to express just how good he has been. Through 31 starts, his 1.95 ERA trails only Ron Guidry’s 1.71 ERA in 1978. His 21 starts of one run or fewer are the most in franchise history. And in the past 11o years, only three pitchers his age or younger have matched him, including Babe Ruth in 1916.
CBSSports | Mike Axisa: Meanwhile, if you hadn’t heard, Aaron Judge is headed back to the IL, this time with a calf injury. In the aftermath of the Captain’s injury, Axisa takes a look at a few questions for Judge, and for the Yankees at large. For Judge, if he can return in time for a playoff run, how much has the injury set him back? Will he be able to find his timing at the dish? For the Yankees, if Judge is out or ineffective, where does that leave the offense against southpaws? It sure would be nice if Judge returns in good order and quickly finds his footing.
The Athletic | Brendan Kuty ($): Speaking of Judge’s calf injury, there’s a little bit of clarification on its nature, if not its severity or a timeline. The injury is in Judge’s inner, lower calf. That part of the calf is important for “sustained activities such as standing or walking uphill.” Judge has previously played through calf injuries. This time, however, it’s in a spot that makes doing so more difficult. So here we are, with the best hitter in the world back on the IL as the Yanks approach the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
Right-handed starting pitcher Cam Schlittler allowed three runs (one earned) on three hits and three walks while striking out six over six innings as the New York Yankees lost 5-3 to the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field in Phoenix on Saturday night.
Pavin Smith hit a walk-off two-run homer to secure the victory for Arizona.
The Yankees fell to five games behind the Tampa Bay Rays for first place in the American League East after the loss.
Schlittler, the clear AL Cy Young favorite, was asked about the Yankees being five games back of the Rays.
New York Yankees Ace Cam Schlittler Makes Honest Statement After Loss to Diamondbacks
The New York Daily News’ Gary Phillips wrote on X:
Cam Schlittler on the #Yankees being 5 games behind the #Rays:
“We gotta go on a good run. It’s gonna be tough. I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job with it. So there’s still a chance, but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
Looking at the New York Yankees
The Yankees have the day off on Monday after they finish their series against the Diamondbacks on Sunday.
On Tuesday, New York is set to begin a four-game series against Tampa Bay, starting with a doubleheader.
At this point, the Yankees likely need to sweep the Rays to win the AL East. After the Rays series, the Yankees will host the Baltimore Orioles for three games, then the postseason will begin.
New York has already clinched a postseason spot, but it’s more likely the club will be a Wild Card team than a division winner.
With an 89-65 record, the Yankees are the first AL Wild Card team. They hold a 5 1/2-game lead over the Boston Red Sox, the second AL Wild Card team.
Most likely, the Yankees will host the Red Sox for a best-of-three Wild Card series. If the Yankees somehow win the AL East, they won’t have to play in the Wild Card round and will automatically earn a spot in the Division round.
The series finale of the three-game set between the Yankees and the Diamondbacks is scheduled to begin at 4:10 p.m. EDT on Sunday. Yankees fans can watch the game on the YES Network.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Yankees' ace just crashed the Cy Young race
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: The Yankees got walked off in Phoenix on Friday. Cam Schlittler was not the reason why. He gave them six innings, one earned run and six strikeouts before the game got away late. At some point, it gets silly to keep calling this a nice first season in the majors. Schlittler has a 1.94 ERA, a 0.91 WHIP and 234 strikeouts across 190 2/3 innings. A line like that belongs at the front of a rotation, and it is happening while everyone is busy checking other names in the award race. I am done treating
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees got walked off in Phoenix on Friday. Cam Schlittler was not the reason why. He gave them six innings, one earned run and six strikeouts before the game got away late.
At some point, it gets silly to keep calling this a nice first season in the majors. Schlittler has a 1.94 ERA, a 0.91 WHIP and 234 strikeouts across 190 2/3 innings. A line like that belongs at the front of a rotation, and it is happening while everyone is busy checking other names in the award race.
I am done treating him like a cute September development. The Yankees have an ace who is already pitching like he belongs in the Cy Young mix.
Friday also put him in unusual company. Schlittler has now allowed one earned run or fewer in 24 starts, an absurdly steady run for a pitcher carrying a real workload.
Why the Yankees’ ace belongs in the Cy Young race
Schlittler has not built the case on one monster outing or a couple of easy matchups. The workload and strikeouts stand up, while the traffic has stayed low enough that even a rough bullpen finish cannot hide how good the starter was again.
The usual experience gap applies. Voters will have other pitchers with longer track records, and awards can become a name-recognition contest when the numbers are close. Still, a 1.94 ERA after nearly 200 innings does not need a sales pitch.
Friday did not damage the argument
The final score will bother Yankees fans more than Schlittler’s line. Arizona beat New York 5-3 on Pavin Smith’s ninth-inning homer, but the loss did not undo what the right-hander gave the club.
Schlittler should get the next start with more than a pat on the back. He has given the Yankees a legitimate Cy Young candidate, and he is making that claim harder to dismiss every five days.
More about:New York Yankees

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Cam Schlittler se fue del Chase Field con otra actuación como lanzador que se consideraría dominante en casi cualquier otro sitio. Para los Yankees, fue otro recordatorio de que un as solo puede compensar hasta cierto punto cuando el margen a su alrededor no deja de reducirse.
Schlittler limitó a Arizona a tres hits y una carrera limpia en seis entradas el sábado por la noche, ponchando a seis y concediendo tres bases por bolas. Aun así , los Yankees perdieron por 5-3 cuando Pavin Smith conectó un jonrón de dos carreras como bateador suplente ante Michael Fulmer en la novena entrada, lo que convirtió un partido empatado en la undécima derrota de Nueva York en la última entrada de la temporada.
Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-65 y a cinco partidos del Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando solo quedan ocho partidos por disputar. Nueva York ya se ha asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero el camino hacia el título de división pasa ahora por cuatro partidos contra los Rays en el Yankee Stadium y necesitará algo de ayuda más allá de esa serie.
La actuación de Schlittler hizo que el resultado fuera más difícil de pasar por alto como una simple derrota de septiembre. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó hasta 1,94, el mejor de la Liga Americana, y sus estadísticas de la temporada quedaron en 14-6, con 234 strikeouts en 190 2/3 entradas. Terminó su gira con un promedio de carreras limpias de 1,16 en 17 partidos como titular.
Los Yankees le dieron una ventaja momentánea de 3-2 en la sexta entrada gracias a dos jonrones solitarios de Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells. Schlittler empezó entonces la parte baja de la entrada con ocho bolas seguidas, Geraldo Perdomo conectó un sencillo de toque y un fly de sacrificio de Corbin Carroll empató el partido. Antes, un error de Schlittler en la defensa ante un toque de Tim Tawa ayudó a que Jordan Lawlar conectara un triple de dos carreras.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria tras lanzar 1 1/3 entradas sin permitir ningún hit con Arizona. Fulmer se llevó la derrota después de que Ildemaro Vargas ganara una revisión de ABS por una base por bolas al primer bateador en la novena y Smith mandara un cutter a las gradas del campo derecho. No hubo salvamento.
Así pues, Schlittler había sumado seis entradas más de excelente control de carreras sin cambiar el problema general de los Yankees. Nueva York acabó con un balance de 20-12 en sus 32 salidas como titular, un balance poco habitual para un equipo que solo ha encajado una carrera limpia o menos en 24 de esas salidas.
La racha histórica de no encajar carreras sigue adentrándose en un terreno cada vez más excepcional
La derrota no frenó el ascenso de Schlittler en las estadísticas. Según la investigación histórica de Sarah Langs, Schlittler acumuló 24 salidas en las que no permitió más de una carrera limpia, lo que le sitúa empatado con Bob Gibson en 1968 y Sandy Koufax en 1966 en el segundo puesto de la «Era de la Bola Viva». Koufax llegó a 25 en 1963.
En la historia de la Liga Americana, solo Walter Johnson logró más salidas de este tipo en una temporada: 27 en 1913 y 26 en 1914. El promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de Schlittler a domicilio, de 1,16, solo queda por detrás del 1,06 de Johnson en 1913 entre los lanzadores de la Liga Americana con al menos 15 salidas como visitante.
Su trayectoria profesional es casi igual de impresionante. En sus primeras 45 salidas como titular en las Grandes Ligas, antes del sábado, Schlittler sumaba 312 strikeouts y una ERA de 2,24. Según los datos históricos que nos han facilitado, se sitúa junto a José Fernández y Paul Skenes como los únicos lanzadores que han superado los 300 ponches sin superar una efectividad de 2,30 hasta ese momento.
Schlittler tiene ahora una media de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de 2,22 en su carrera, con 318 strikeouts en 46 partidos como titular. Además, está intentando unirse a Ron Guidry en 1978 y a Spud Chandler en 1943 como los únicos lanzadores titulares de los Yankees de la «era de la bola viva» que han terminado una temporada con una efectividad por debajo de 2,00.
Schlittler lanza un mensaje contundente
No fue hasta después del partido cuando Schlittler pasó de hablar de sus propias estadísticas de lanzamiento a hablar de la posición de los Yankees en la clasificación. Cuando le preguntaron por la diferencia de cinco partidos, hizo un análisis directo de una carrera en la que Nueva York ha tenido varias oportunidades de recortar distancias.
«Tenemos que encadenar una buena racha. Va a ser duro. Creo que hemos tenido oportunidades durante toda la temporada para ponernos por delante, y no las hemos aprovechado muy bien. Así que todavía hay posibilidades, pero tenemos que darlo todo».
El mensaje cobró aún más importancia porque Schlittler acababa de asumir la responsabilidad de la jugada que le había cambiado el comienzo del partido. No utilizó las dos carreras no ganadas como excusa para que los Yankees perdieran otro partido que necesitaban ganar.
«Bueno, no diría que les di una oportunidad de verdad», dijo Schlittler. «Eso es culpa mía, así que asumo la responsabilidad. Cometí un error ahí y les dejé marcar dos carreras».
Reiteró esa idea unos instantes después, en lugar de echarle la culpa a la defensa, al bullpen o a la alineación.
«Bueno, así es el béisbol, pero sí, esa la pago yo».
Una jugada maestra más podría decidir cómo empieza octubre
Un gráfico comparativo de la MLB publicado antes del sábado situaba la temporada de Schlittler al mismo nivel que la de Clayton Kershaw en 2014, cuando fue MVP, y la de Justin Verlander en 2011, también como MVP. Esa comparación refleja hasta qué punto su candidatura ha ido más allá de la típica discusión sobre el premio Cy Young, aunque la carrera por el MVP siga siendo otra historia.
Para los Yankees, lo más importante ahora mismo es octubre. Los Yankees pueden armar su rotación para la postemporada en torno a Schlittler, que está listo para encabezar esa rotación, y Nueva York puede alinearlo para una salida más en la temporada regular, posiblemente contra Tampa Bay durante la serie de cuatro partidos que empieza el martes.
Su valoración sin rodeos después de que Arizona demostrara más que nadie la urgencia del momento. Los Yankees siguen contando con su mejor lanzador, que está rindiendo a un nivel histórico. Lo que sigue siendo una incógnita es si le han dejado suficientes partidos para dar un giro a la lucha por el título de división.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Yankees’ division dreams hanging by a thread after walk-off loss: ‘It’s gonna be tough’
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: PHOENIX — Both the Yankees and Rays saw their respective games end in walk-off fashion on Saturday, but only one of the division rivals emerged victorious. It wasn’t the Yanks, who suffered a 5-3 loss to the Diamondbacks when Michael Fulmer surrendered a game-ending, two-run home to Pavin Smith with one out in the ninth inning. Aaron Boone said that he considered using Clarke Schmidt, one game back from Tommy John surgery, instead, but he went with the journeyman Fulmer because he’s had more exp
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Both the Yankees and Rays saw their respective games end in walk-off fashion on Saturday, but only one of the division rivals emerged victorious.
It wasn’t the Yanks, who suffered a 5-3 loss to the Diamondbacks when Michael Fulmer surrendered a game-ending, two-run home to Pavin Smith with one out in the ninth inning. Aaron Boone said that he considered using Clarke Schmidt, one game back from Tommy John surgery, instead, but he went with the journeyman Fulmer because he’s had more experience in those situations.
“I just felt like Fulmer’s been in these spots and throwing the ball really well for us, and Smith got him there,” Boone said of the reliever, who has a 3.09 ERA this season.
Meanwhile, at Tropicana Field, the Rays pulled off a 2-1 win over the Red Sox thanks to a bloop single from Richie Palacios in the ninth. Tampa now has a five-game lead over the Yankees with just eight games left in the regular season.
The American League East foes will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium from Sept. 22-24, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday. Boone acknowledged that his club will probably have to sweep the Rays for a crack at a division title.
“We sweep, then it gets interesting,” the manager said with the Yankees’ postseason ticket already punched.
But the odds are already stacked against the Yankees with the team finishing its series in Arizona on Sunday. They entered Saturday with a just a 2.8% chance of winning the division, according to FanGraphs.
Making matters tougher is that the Rays, owners of the AL’s best record, currently lead the season series between the two teams, 6-3. There’s also the fact that the Yankees will be without Aaron Judge, who returned to the injured list with calf strain on Saturday.
“They’re playing tremendous baseball, so it’s tough to climb up in the standings when they keep winning,” Cody Bellinger said after going 0-for-4 on Saturday. “So mathematically, it’s pretty tough, but gotta keep on rolling.”
“We gotta go on a good run. It’s gonna be tough,” added Cam Schlittler, who allowed one earned run over six innings but committed a costly error on Saturday. “I think we’ve had opportunities all season to put ourselves ahead, and we haven’t done a great job with it. So there’s still a chance, but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
The good news for the Yankees is that their best starters are lined up to face the Rays. While they haven’t officially announced their probables for the series, it looks like Max Fried and Carlos Rodón will pitch the doubleheader before Gerrit Cole and Schlittler, the Cy Young frontrunner, close out the four-game set.
The Rays, however, are set to throw a few of their best with Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez, Ian Seymour and Freddy Peralta slotted for the highly-anticipated matchup.
While they’re not officially out of the division race yet, the likeliest scenario is that the Yankees end up hosting Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year. It is not where the team wants to end up after finishing 2025 with the same record as the Blue Jays but losing the season series tiebreaker, but Bellinger remained confident that the Yankees can still win their first title since 2009.
“Obviously, the goal is to win the division, rest your guys, get those extra off days,” he said. “That’s always goal No. 1. Ultimately, World Series champions have come out of the Wild Card.”

item.title: [courant.com] Dom Amore’s Sunday Read: Coach that launched Sun has his day; big skates to fill at UConn, and more
item.dc:creator: Dom Amore
item.description: Mike Thibault was with the Lakers during the early 1980s “Showtime” period, and he was with the Bulls when they drafted Michael Jordan. Then he moved around to different leagues, circumstances, and went back to the NBA as a Bucks assistant. In 2003, he signed on to be the head coach the original Portland Fire of the WNBA, but Paul Allen, one of the richest men on earth, folded the franchise.
