item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Cam Schlittler gets interesting MVP update from ESPN analyst originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees don't have Aaron Judge tearing it up and contending for the AL MVP this season, and while Ben Rice has been great, his odds for the award are slim due to his lackluster value defensively.
But that doesn't mean the Yankees don't have someone in contention for the AL MVP award. ESPN analyst Bradford Doolittle does have an advanced statistic that has placed Cam Schlittler near the top of the MVP standings.
While it might still be a long shot for Schlittler to win the AL MVP, Doolittle's "AXE" rating has Schlittler second only to Yordan Alvarez, and not by much, in the AL MVP race.
Cam Schlittler is currently No. 2 in the MVP ranking by an ESPN analyst
"Front-runner: Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros (146.9 AXE). Next nine: 2, Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees (143.0)," Doolittle writes.
While Doolittle noted that Schlittler has an "uphill battle" to winning the AL MVP, it's not completely out of the question just yet.
With a lack of a true runaway favorite in the AL MVP race, even with Alvarez contending for the AL Triple Crown, Schlittler's chances are much better than they normally might be.
He's been dominant this season and is the favorite, according to Doolittle, to win the AL Cy Young Award. The MVP award is significantly more difficult for Schlittler to win, and it'd take a near-perfect set of circumstances for him to have a chance at this honor.
In 31 starts this season, Schlittler has a 1.95 ERA and 7.1 bWAR. To win the AL MVP, he'd need to make at least one more start, likely a lengthy one without allowing a run, and to take the MLB ERA title, not just the AL ERA title.
Even if he were to pitch a perfect game in his final start of the year, he would need two other things to happen to win this AL MVP award.
The first would be for Alvarez to lose the Triple Crown while the Astros miss out on the playoffs. The other would be for Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays to have a terrible final few games of the year and drop the Rays out of the AL East lead.
All in all, it's nearly impossible for Schlittler to end the 2026 season as the AL MVP. But considering that pitchers never have a chance for this award, the fact that Doolittle is even willing to name him as a candidate is a testament to how great he's been this season.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Cam Schlittler, Yanks continue playoff push in clash against Mets
item.description: Starting pitcher Gerrit Cole described the New York Yankees playing games in September as the postseason approaches as “the fun part” while Francisco Lindor lamented how the New York Mets did not do enough early this season to put themselves in contention for the playoffs. On Saturday, the Yankees’ quest to clinch a postseason spot was partially derailed by the Mets continuing their late hot streak after falling out of contention earlier in the season. After a rough performance Saturday and with
item.content:encoded:
Starting pitcher Gerrit Cole described the New York Yankees playing games in September as the postseason approaches as “the fun part” while Francisco Lindor lamented how the New York Mets did not do enough early this season to put themselves in contention for the playoffs.
On Saturday, the Yankees’ quest to clinch a postseason spot was partially derailed by the Mets continuing their late hot streak after falling out of contention earlier in the season.
After a rough performance Saturday and with American League Cy Young Award favorite Cam Schlittler on the mound Sunday afternoon, the Yankees will attempt to move toward securing their ninth playoff appearance in 10 seasons when they host the Mets in the season finale of the Subway Series.
The Yankees (85-63) are 17-8 in their past 25 games despite allowing six homers in Saturday’s 12-2 loss to the Mets. Cole allowed three homers in 4 1/3 innings before the Yankees took one of their worst defeats this season.
“This is the fun part of it, because the reward is close,” he said. “Getting to the postseason, being able to chase your ultimate goal — these are the games you look forward to the most.”
With 14 games left, the Yankees begin Sunday needing a win, and then a loss by the Toronto Blue Jays, to join the Los Angeles Dodgers as the only teams to make the playoffs in nine of the past 10 seasons since 2017.
The Mets (69-79), meanwhile, are trying to fend off clinching a losing season for as long as possible after falling 19 games under .500 in July, losing 12 straight in April, and trading several players at the Aug. 3 trade deadline.
Since the trades, the Mets are 22-13 and are coming off setting a Subway Series record with six homers on Saturday. The team also is 5-1 in its past six games, collecting 51 runs, 17 homers and batting .279.
Lindor, who missed two months of the season with a calf injury and is hitting .234, is coming off a big showing with a leadoff homer off Cole and a grand slam in the eighth. Lindor has four of his five multi-homer games since Aug. 30 and heads into his first encounter against Schlittler batting .314 in 26 Subway Series games since joining the Mets in 2021.
“This is what we should have been doing from the beginning, but it’s part of the journey and part of the year and try to make the most of it,” Lindor said.
Said Mets interim manager Andy Green: “We didn’t meet expectations for the vast majority of the season, but where this group is mentally right now, when we step on the field, we expect to win. We don’t really care who’s on the other side.”
Schlittler (13-6, 2.01 ERA), who leads the majors by allowing one earned run or less in 20 starts, will face the Mets for the second time in his career. He has allowed one run or less in his past six starts since Aug. 3 and has 49 strikeouts in those games.
Schlittler last pitched on Tuesday, when he allowed one run on three hits and struck out 10 in a 5-3 win over the Colorado Rockies.
In his only appearance against the Mets, on May 15 at Citi Field, he allowed one run on two hits in 6 2/3 innings and earned the victory when he also struck out nine while Lindor was on the injured list. The Yankees won 5-2.
After getting seven impressive innings Saturday from Zac Thornton (two runs over seven innings), the Mets will start their third rookie of the series when right-hander Christian Scott (4-4, 3.81 ERA) faces the Yankees for the first time.
Scott most recently pitched in last Sunday’s 4-2 win over the San Francisco Giants, when he allowed two runs on four hits in 4 2/3 innings before the Mets scored four times in the eighth inning.
–Field Level Media

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] 25 starts later, Carlos Rodón has made the Yankees' October call uncomfortable
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: There is a point where a nice stretch stops being a nice stretch. Carlos Rodón has crossed that line for the Yankees. Rodón gave them six innings, two earned runs and five strikeouts on Wednesday in Minnesota. The 5-4 loss took some shine off the afternoon, but his start extended a run that is getting hard to brush aside: 25 straight outings with no more than three runs allowed and no more than one homer surrendered. He does not have to start Game 1. Max Fried and Cam Schlittler have been excell
item.content:encoded:
There is a point where a nice stretch stops being a nice stretch. Carlos Rodón has crossed that line for the Yankees.
Rodón gave them six innings, two earned runs and five strikeouts on Wednesday in Minnesota. The 5-4 loss took some shine off the afternoon, but his start extended a run that is getting hard to brush aside: 25 straight outings with no more than three runs allowed and no more than one homer surrendered.
He does not have to start Game 1. Max Fried and Cam Schlittler have been excellent, and October is not a participation trophy for everybody who had a good September. The rotation conversation cannot be handled with old assumptions anymore.
The Yankees have a real surplus of starters who can make a case. It is a good issue to have, but the first series is short and the opponent decides who gets the ball after the opener.
The Yankees have to count the whole body of work
Rodón’s recent run is not built on smoke. He has kept the ball in the yard, limited crooked innings, and worked deep enough into games to spare the bullpen. Wednesday was not perfect, with three walks and 102 pitches, yet he gave New York a clean six-inning start while the game was still there for the taking.
October asks for exactly that kind of start. Nobody needs a masterpiece every time; they need someone who can keep a game in the middle innings without handing the other dugout a free runway.
I would not overreact to one loss in Minneapolis. I would react to the 25-start sample, because it now carries real weight in the Yankees’ season.
Carlos Rodón has earned a real say in October
The reasonable answer may be matchups. A left-handed lineup could push Rodón up the board, while a series schedule might make a different order cleaner. Fine. The Yankees should use every edge they can find.
What they should not do is treat Rodón like the interchangeable third or fourth starter just because that was easier to say months ago. His work has made the pecking order less tidy. Good pitchers tend to do that.
The rotation debate is not settled, and it should not be. Rodón has made sure it will be an actual decision instead of a formality.
More about:New York Yankees

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Yankees' Cam Schlittler, Rays' Junior Caminero Are Crashing Yordan Alvarez's AL MVP Party
item.dc:creator: Zachary D Rymer
item.description: Yankees' Cam Schlittler, Rays' Junior Caminero Are Crashing Yordan Alvarez's AL MVP Party Welcome to MLB's potentially permanent post-Aaron Judge MVP landscape. Now it's a three-horse AL MVP race, still undecided even in the last 10 days of the season. It's Yordan Alvarez vs. Junior Caminero vs. Cam Schlittler. Choose your fighter. If there is a favorite, it's Alvarez. He's had one hand on the AL MVP for most of the season, and FanDuel is ready to assume he'll eventually get the other hand on it
item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Cam Schlittler, Rays' Junior Caminero Are Crashing Yordan Alvarez's AL MVP Party
Welcome to MLB's potentially permanent post-Aaron Judge MVP landscape. Now it's a three-horse AL MVP race, still undecided even in the last 10 days of the season.
It's Yordan Alvarez vs. Junior Caminero vs. Cam Schlittler. Choose your fighter.
If there is a favorite, it's Alvarez. He's had one hand on the AL MVP for most of the season, and FanDuel is ready to assume he'll eventually get the other hand on it. Here are their current odds:
TOP NEWS
Brutal Mets x Alonso Stat 🤢
Every Team's Biggest Offseason Decision 🧐
Yanks Could Be LOADED Next Year 😤
- Yordan Alvarez, Houston Astros: -20000
- Junior Caminero, Tampa Bay Rays: +1400
- Cam Schlittler, New York Yankees: +7000
- Bobby Witt Jr., Kansas City Royals: +10000
However, the tide is turning. Yankees manager Aaron Boone is openly pondering whether Schlittler deserves the MVP. And after hitting two walk-off home runs in four games, Caminero has turned a low hum of an MVP case into a loud scream.
Is this an erasure of what Alvarez has done? Or are there genuine cases for Caminero and Schlittler? Let's discuss.
Yordan Alvarez's AL MVP Case Is Ironclad… Sort Of
The Gist: He leads the AL in everything, but his case does break down upon examination.
Alvarez came into 2026 with a conundrum. He was clearly one of baseball's best hitters, yet he had never led the AL in any key statistical category.
Talk about making up for lost time. The 29-year-old has stayed healthy and mashed all year, resulting in AL-leading marks in:
- AVG: .310
- OBP: .428
- SLG: .594
- OPS: 1.022
- OPS+: 188
Alvarez also has 39 home runs and 98 RBI, putting him just two and four off the AL-leading paces set by Caminero and Pete Alonso. We're still on Triple Crown watch with Alvarez.
There's just one problem: Alvarez has gone kind of cold.
That is, "cold" relative to his own standards. Through the end of July, Alvarez had a 1.077 OPS and 35 homers. Since August 1, he has a .860 OPS with four homers. Nick Sogard has more homers since then, and he began his major league career with 252 plate appearances without going deep even once.
If this year's MVP voters want to hold the AL West against Alvarez, that wouldn't be unfair. It's a historically bad division, and Alvarez has benefited to the tune of an MLB-high 447 plate appearances against teams with losing records through play on Tuesday.
He has a 1.118 OPS against those teams, compared to a .817 OPS against all others. That's an unflattering 301-point gap.
Junior Caminero Has the Vibes
The Gist: There's more here than just the home runs.
Caminero's 41 homers are the only true statistical advantage he has over Alvarez. Unless, of course, you want to count double plays grounded into. For the second year in a row, Caminero leads in that category, too.
Aside from that, Alvarez has a 1.024 OPS vs. Caminero's .897 OPS. It's also Alvarez's 6.1 rWAR vs. Caminero's 5.6 rWAR.
So what does Caminero's AL MVP case come down to? Vibes, mostly.
There's only a minuscule difference between Caminero's performance against losing teams (.908 OPS) and winning teams (.880 OPS). That has mattered to a Rays squad that built its AL-best 92-59 record in part by going 38-24 against other winning teams.
This is a form of clutchness in itself, and some argue it matters more than Alvarez's generic blend of clutchness. Even there, the comparison between the two is basically Great vs. Greater. In high-leverage spots, for example, Caminero has a .958 OPS to Alvarez's 1.190 OPS. Nothing wrong with either one.
The other side of the ball matters, too. Caminero hasn't started even one game at designated hitter, compared to 126 for Alvarez. While Caminero hardly has a sterling reputation at third base, Mike Petriello of MLB.com noted that he has moved into positive territory in Fielding Run Value since the start of June.
Cam Schlittler Is More Than an Also-Ran
The Gist: According to one stat, he should be the favorite.
Aaron Judge? He knows a thing or three about MVP awards. So what does he think about the Yankees' right-handed ace winning it this year?
"They've got a Cy Young Award for a reason—best pitcher in the game," Judge said, per Chris Kirschner of The Athletic. "He's got my vote, definitely, for the Cy Young."
Harsh… but fair? Not if you look at Schlittler's ranks on the AL leaderboard! He's the leader in:
- ERA: 1.95
- ERA+: 216
- WHIP: 0.904
- WAR: 7.0
Those first three are impressive marks for a pitcher. That last one is impressive, period. By rWAR, Schlittler literally is the most valuable player in the AL.
This isn't necessarily an automatic mic drop for MVP voters. As Brian Murphy of MLB.com noted, eight full-time pitchers have led the AL in rWAR over the last 30 years, and only one (Justin Verlander in 2011) won the MVP.
Context matters, though. In this case, Schlittler has been a constant in a season otherwise marked by turmoil for the Yankees. He's allowed two earned runs or fewer in 25 of his 31 starts, making him the only pitcher who can claim that. The Yankees are 19-6 in those games.
Predicting Who Comes Out on Top
The Gist: It could be close.
Here's the thing about Alvarez as the heavy AL MVP favorite: He's the favorite because he should be.
We talked about the numbers. What we didn't talk about is how screwed the Astros would be without him. For example, they are 20-14 in games where he's hit at least one home run. Eliminate or greatly reduce those 34 games, and they're not hanging onto the AL West lead with a 76-76 record.
It should also work in Alvarez's favor that there isn't a united front behind Caminero or Schlittler. They could end up merely splitting whatever votes don't go to Alvarez. And if any of the three is going to get more than one-third of the bunch, it's probably Alvarez.
Even so, it's hard to ignore the feeling that Alvarez's case is more precarious than it should be.
Whereas his MVP creds peaked in July and have been in stasis ever since, Caminero and Schlittler have been busy strengthening theirs. They also play on better teams in a better division that tends to have more eyes on it. I'm told they call it "East Coast bias."
Nobody likes boring predictions, so here goes with a bold call for how the AL MVP voting will play out:
- Junior Caminero
- Yordan Alvarez
- Cam Schlittler
I'm caught between thinking Caminero shouldn't win it and thinking he shouldn't not win it. What's clear is that he wants the AL MVP and is pushing hard for it. Those two walk-offs are just two of four homers he's hit in his last 10 games. It doesn't make for a bad narrative that it's service of a Rays team that is outpacing a Yankees team that is spending three times as much money on payroll.
So, congratulations to Junior Caminero. Or, sorry for the jinx. It depends on what actually happens.

item.title: [nytimes.com] The MLB prospects I was wrong about: Jacob Misiorowski, Ben Rice and more
item.dc:creator: Keith Law
item.description: At the end of every season, I look at players who’ve succeeded in the major leagues beyond the expectations I had for them, and explain where my projections went wrong. Sometimes it’s what I saw (or didn’t see); sometimes it’s a matter of incomplete information from sources, but regardless of the reasons, they’re my mistakes, and it’s on me to learn from them to improve my projections for other players who might show similarities to these players in the future. item.content:encoded:
At the end of every season, I look at players who’ve succeeded in the major leagues beyond the expectations I had for them, and explain where my projections went wrong. Sometimes it’s what I saw (or didn’t see); sometimes it’s a matter of incomplete information from sources, but regardless of the reasons, they’re my mistakes, and it’s on me to learn from them to improve my projections for other players who might show similarities to these players in the future.
Advertisement
I do have some general criteria for this list, as I look for players who have become regulars, either as everyday position players or bona fide starting pitchers, where I thought they’d be bench players, relievers or something less. In most cases, I look for more than one year of sustained performance at this higher level. These aren’t the only players I got wrong, for sure, but I’ve covered some in previous editions of this article (here’s last year’s and 2024’s), and I’d also rather go a little deeper on guys I got more wrong or where I can tell a clear story of why I got them wrong.
Regardless, here are a few new players where I was way too low on my projections for their major-league careers.
Jacob Misiorowski, RHP, Milwaukee Brewers
I know I wasn’t alone in my belief that Misiorowski wouldn’t hold up as a starter, either because he wouldn’t throw enough strikes or because he would break down. No one has ever thrown this hard, this much, without getting hurt. Jordan Hicks couldn’t do it. Aroldis Chapman couldn’t do it. Hunter Greene just underwent Tommy John surgery for the second time. Ben Joyce can’t even hold up in relief.
The Brewers took Misiorowski in the second round in 2022 out of a junior college (Crowder College), where he started the spring walking a batter an inning but brought that down as the season progressed. While at school, he was already touching 100 mph with a plus slider and great extension out front.
The delivery was still quite rough, and even with the benefit of some of the best stuff in the minors, he still walked almost 15 percent of batters during his time in Double A in 2023 and 2024. He was so inefficient that he’d hit his pitch limits before getting through five innings in the majority of his outings.
His control took another step forward in Triple A to start the 2025 season, and now, improbably, he’s walking just 6.6 percent of batters in the big leagues while throwing harder than any starter in history and doing it with a cleaner, much more repeatable delivery.
Advertisement
There are some small mechanical changes at play in Misiorowski’s ascent, but nothing strikes me as bigger than the fact that he has gotten so much stronger since he was drafted, particularly in his lower half. He’s striding and landing more consistently, and he’s not falling off nearly as hard to the first-base side. When he was in junior college, he’d be lucky to see the plate when he released the ball, with his head snapping hard down to his left at release.
Now he’s throwing harder while looking like he’s expending less effort, which seems hard to believe given that he’s been up to 105 mph and is setting all kinds of records in the pitch-tracking era for velocity. His “Maddux” against the Phillies in May, where he struck out 15, gave up one hit and no other baserunners, and still hit 103.7 mph in the ninth inning, is one of the best pitching performances I’ve ever watched. The Phillies looked like they were swinging toothpicks.
Misiorowski’s development wasn’t accident, but rather the culmination of efforts the Brewers undertook from the moment he joined their organization. After the draft, the Brewers worked right away to get more stability into Misiorowski’s delivery, and to improve his direction so he could be more online to the plate, especially since stuff like his will play in the zone. They also made small changes to simplify the delivery so it would be easier for him to repeat, which might be part of why his stuff has trended upwards if that helped make the delivery more efficient.
He worked with a huge group of Brewers coaches throughout the minors and in the big leagues, including pitching coordinator Nick Childs, assistant pitching coordinator Bryan Leslie and current Giants pitching coach Justin Meccage, who was the pitching coach for Triple-A Nashville last year when Misiorowski started the season there. (Meccage’s nephew, Bryce, is a pitcher in the Brewers’ system.) I thought any team would try to smooth out Miz’s delivery, but that either it would cost him velocity — that the power was the result of the violence, not held back by it, because who thinks a guy throwing 100 could actually be throwing harder if he had better mechanics? — or that it wouldn’t improve his control enough to keep him a starter. Obviously, that didn’t end up being the case. His delivery and command improved and he maintained his elite velocity.
In this annual series, I often try to highlight how I might evaluate a similar prospect differently in the future. In Misiorowski’s case, I don’t know if there’s a lesson to be learned other than it is possible, with n of 1, that a human being can throw this hard this much and be a successful starter, at least for two years, without getting hurt. That’s one datum against all of the pitchers in history who’ve thrown close to this hard and either haven’t held up — Greene’s second Tommy John surgery is the result of at least his third major arm injury — or have had to move to the bullpen, like the other guys I mentioned above. Even Paul Skenes has seen his velocity taper this year.
Advertisement
The base rate for pitchers with this kind of outsized velocity and higher walk rates when younger is still overwhelmingly in the direction of them not sticking as starters. Misiorowski is a unicorn, or a black swan, who at least has shown that staying healthy and throwing strikes with the hardest fastball in history is possible.
Ben Rice, DH/1B/C, New York Yankees
Rice was barely a prospect at all coming up in the Yankees’ system. He was a 2021 12th-round pick out of Dartmouth, where he hit one homer in 30 games (losing almost two seasons to the pandemic).
Even when he started producing in the minor leagues, with a 20-homer season across three levels in 2023, he was old for the levels he played at and didn’t have a position — he was a catcher with no shot to stay there. His swing was extremely uphill, prioritizing power over everything else, and in his first stint in the majors in 2024, pitchers exploited that swing path, leading to his first struggles in pro ball.
Rice went out that offseason and worked on his swing and his body, gaining enough strength to improve his bat speed and, naturally, his contact quality. It wasn’t his first rodeo — he’d changed his stance and swing while in college — but this change was more dramatic, with a much more open setup and a stride that didn’t close himself off, helping him roll over to the right side less often and, at least in 2025, pull the ball in the air more.
The change also made him less vulnerable on stuff middle-in; in 2024, he whiffed on 25 percent of pitches on the inner third, then cut that to 11.3 percent in 2025 and 11.9 percent so far this year. He’s still not a catcher, but he’s a top-10 bat in the majors this year.
I also didn’t have Rice’s teammate, Cam Schlittler, performing as he has in the majors, not when I saw his career-worst outing in Triple A right before he got called up, and not any time before that. He barely threw a sinker at all when I saw him, and used it just 6.1 percent of the time in the majors last year, but this year he’s used it 19.6 percent of the time. Schlittler has thrown something other than one of his three fastballs just 10.6 percent of the time this year. Only Chad Patrick throws fewer non-fastballs among starters with 100+ innings this year; Misiorowski is fourth on the list at 18.3 percent.
Otto Lopez, SS, Miami Marlins
I knew Lopez could play shortstop — that was pretty consistent across all sources — but never had him as a plus defender there. The Blue Jays, his original organization, didn’t seem to view him that way, and ended up selling his contract to the Giants, who then put him on waivers two months later, at which point the Marlins claimed him. And then Miami started him out as their second baseman, where he was a plus defender right away, then moved him to shortstop in 2025 and gave him that job full-time this year, where he’s at plus-10 Outs Above Average with a few weeks to go in the season.
At the plate, he’s always put the ball in play a lot, which I thought would make him a utility infielder, but I wrote before the 2023 season that “he lacks the power or even the impact to be a regular.” That was proven wrong pretty quickly, as even in 2024 he posted a 92 wRC+, close enough to a league-average bat that he was worth over 2 WAR in both the FanGraphs and Baseball-Reference systems. This year, he’s boosted his contact quality even further, with a career-best 40.5 percent hard-hit rate, producing a 116 wRC+ and over 5 WAR already.
Advertisement
I just missed on this one — I was way off on the defense and too light on the offense, treating him like a Nick Madrigal-type hitter who wouldn’t hit the ball hard enough to make his contact ability matter.
Kyle Leahy, RHP, St. Louis Cardinals
I saw Leahy in the Arizona Fall League in 2022, where he posted a 10.67 ERA in 14 1/3 innings, writing afterward that he was a “possible reliever” who was 93-96 with a “decent curveball” and a slider, not mentioning a changeup (I doubt I even saw one) or sweeper.
He’d been a starter that season in Double A, but wasn’t good by any measure. He walked a batter every other inning (11.1 percent) and gave up 22 homers in 141 innings, ending up with an ERA of 5.23. That, oddly enough, was an improvement over 2025, when he was also in Double A and posted an 8.20 ERA, losing his rotation spot in mid-June.
One of the biggest changes for Leahy from his time in the bullpen is that he started pitching in the strike zone more and, of course, brought his walk rate down. In 2024-25, when he made just one start and 111 relief appearances between Triple A and the majors, he walked 45 batters in 164 2/3 innings (6.7 percent). Another change is that he’s ramped up his use of his changeup, using it about 50 percent more often this year than he did in 2025, which was almost twice what he did in 2023, his first year working primarily in relief. Some of his stuff has clearly backed up this year; the curveball was a plus pitch in 2025, but its spin rate is down, and the pitch is breaking less in both directions, so the slider has become his best pitch.
I’m still skeptical about Leahy in the long term; lefties have smoked him this year for a .312/.379/.473 line, and while it’s great that he’s using his changeup more, it’s not that effective of a pitch. But he belongs on this list because I didn’t think there was any way he could go from “excellent 1-2 inning reliever” to “league-average starter,” nor did I think he’d be a starter back in his prospect days.

item.title: [nytimes.com] Yankees mailbag: Aaron Judge’s injury, Jasson Domínguez’s future and the playoff rotation
item.dc:creator: Chris Kirschner
item.description: The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode. Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

item.title: [Field Level Media] Cam Schlittler dominant as Yankees shut out Mets
item.description: Cam Schlittler pitched six innings of one-hit ball in his latest stellar outing, and the host New York Yankees earned a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets in the final game of the Subway Series on Sunday afternoon. Ben Rice and Austin Wells provided the only runs of the game via solo home runs as the Yankees (86-63) won for the 18th time in 26 games and lowered their magic number for clinching a postseason spot to one. Schlittler allowed only Brett Baty’s double with two outs in the fifth. It wa
item.content:encoded:
Cam Schlittler pitched six innings of one-hit ball in his latest stellar outing, and the host New York Yankees earned a 2-0 victory over the New York Mets in the final game of the Subway Series on Sunday afternoon.
Ben Rice and Austin Wells provided the only runs of the game via solo home runs as the Yankees (86-63) won for the 18th time in 26 games and lowered their magic number for clinching a postseason spot to one.
Schlittler allowed only Brett Baty’s double with two outs in the fifth. It was the third time in his 45 career starts that Schlittler allowed one hit and the second time this season.
Schlittler struck out eight and walked two. He moved into a tie with Milwaukee’s Jacob Misiorowski for the major league lead by lowering his ERA to 1.95 ERA.
Schlittler threw 60 of 94 pitches for strikes and ended his outing after taking Bo Bichette’s comebacker off the back of his right leg. The ball deflected to catcher Wells, who threw to Luis Garcia Jr. at first base to complete the out.
Afterwards, Schlittler headed straight to the clubhouse but seemed fine.
Rice slugged his third career leadoff homer and Wells homered in the third off Mets starter Christian Scott (4-5).
Scott allowed two runs on three hits in six innings. The right-hander struck out Aaron Judge three times and finished with seven strikeouts to go with two walks.
Judge went 0-for-3 and is 3-for-17 since being activated from the IL.
The Yankees’ Brent Headrick tossed a 1-2-3 seventh and Paul Blackburn got Lindor on a pop-up to end the eighth. David Bednar stranded a runner and notched his 34th save in 37 chances.
The Mets (69-80) were blanked for the 14th time as Lindor and Juan Soto were a combined 0-for-7 with four strikeouts.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
With the postseason less than two weeks away, the Yankees are left holding their breath regarding the status of their slugging captain, Aaron Judge, who left Wednesday’s game against the Minnesota Twins early with what the team described as right lower-leg tightness.
Judge, who started the game in right field, was seen wincing during his second and final at-bat of the afternoon in the top of the third inning following a check-swing. He was pinch-hit for by Heliot Ramos in the top of the sixth, sending up immediate red flags for a team fighting to catch the Tampa Bay Rays for the top spot in the American League East.
Manager Aaron Boone said that Juge felt something in the first inning and took him out to make sure he didn’t “push through anything.”
He will undergo treatment, and the team will get a better sense of how severe the issue is on Thursday.
There may be some relief in that it is not his rib or oblique that is bothering him, though such a statement is a bit premature, considering the specifics of this lower-leg issue is unknown. Judge has already missed three months this season due to a rib injury that kept him out from late May to Sept. 7.
Wednesday’s game was just his seventh game back from the injured list, and he has struggled mightily after the long layoff, going 4-for-23 (.173) with one home run, three RBI, and 13 strikeouts.
Boone previously stated that he was going to take things slow with Judge because they forewent a rehab assignment. But he played six straight games before getting Tuesday off — the day after New York clinched its ninth postseason berth in 10 years.
The prospect of being without Judge this postseason should be a daunting one for the Yankees. Their offense struggled mightily without him, scoring 341 runs in the 84 games without him (4.06 runs per game). Only the Cincinnati Reds, Toronto Blue Jays, Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Angels, and Seattle Mariners scored fewer runs in all of baseball during that stretch.
Still, the Bronx Bombers should like their chances regardless of the status of their captain. The American League is exceptionally poor this season, with only six teams possessing records over .500. Three of them, including the Yankees, inhabit the AL East.
They also have one of the most imposing pitching staffs in all of baseball, as they are set to trot out AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodon in a shortened postseason rotation.

item.title: [foxsports.com] Yankees RHP Clarke Schmidt Returns As Reliever After 14-Month Rehab
item.description: Yankees RHP Clarke Schmidt Returns As Reliever After 14-Month Rehab The New York Yankees returned right-handed pitcher Clarke Schmidt from his rehabilitation assignment and reinstated him from the injured list on Wednesday, aiming to integrate the 30-year-old into their bullpen for the postseason following his 14-month recovery from elbow surgery. Schmidt had an internal brace procedure on his ulnar collateral ligament on July 11, 2025, and began minor league rehab on Aug. 29. The 2017 first-rou
item.content:encoded:
Yankees RHP Clarke Schmidt Returns As Reliever After 14-Month Rehab
The New York Yankees returned right-handed pitcher Clarke Schmidt from his rehabilitation assignment and reinstated him from the injured list on Wednesday, aiming to integrate the 30-year-old into their bullpen for the postseason following his 14-month recovery from elbow surgery.
Schmidt had an internal brace procedure on his ulnar collateral ligament on July 11, 2025, and began minor league rehab on Aug. 29. The 2017 first-round draft pick was used exclusively as a starter since 2023, but with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon and Gerrit Cole in the rotation, Schmidt will transition to relief.
"It's been a long journey, a lot of work that goes into this. A lot of long days, early mornings," Schmidt said before the game Wednesday against the Minnesota Twins. "I've just been itching to come back."
The Yankees designated popular multi-position player Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment to make room on the 40-man roster for Schmidt. Cabrera missed most of the 2025 season with a severe ankle injury.
"I’m blessed to have a lot of guys on this team that you just admire and respect and love doing the job with on a daily basis," manager Aaron Boone said. "Oswaldo’s right there at the top of that list."
Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: [theleadsm.com] Cam Schlittler Has a Strong Case for MVP
item.dc:creator: James Nolan

In fact, ESPN’s award tracker no longer has odds for the race. item.content:encoded:
The American League Cy Young race is over. In his last start, Cam Schlittler twirled a six-inning, one-hit, eight-strikeout gem against the Mets. In fact, ESPN’s award tracker no longer has odds for the race.
With the Yankees also clinching a playoff berth with their win Monday night, there’s not much left at stake in New York’s regular season. Except for Schlittler’s potential run at being the first pitcher to win MVP since 2014.
Schlittler has two starts remaining this year. Barring Aaron Boone toying with the rotation to line them up for the postseason, he’s scheduled to get the ball for game two in Arizona on Sept. 19 and game four against the Rays on Sept. 24.
The Statistical Case
There’s a long list of stats you can cite to put Schlittler’s dominance this season in context. There are a few worth highlighting.
Schlittler’s ERA is currently an AL-best 1.95. That’s the lowest ERA of any qualified Yankees starter since Ron Guidry (1.74)in 1978. The next most recent sub-two ERA in Yankee history is 1943 Spud Chandler (1.64). He also has a marginally better ERA than Jacob Misiorowski, the NL frontrunner for Cy Young.
While they both display a 1.95 ERA, the formula for ERA actually allows for the
Schlittler also has a better ERA+ than .
ERA+ adjusts to the league, wherein league average is always 100. That means Schlittler has been 116% better than league average, while Kershaw was “only” 97% better. Schlittler has also done this in 31 starts, while Kershaw has done it in only 27.
Finally, he currently leads the American League in Wins Above Replacement. Yordan Alvarez (5.8), the odds-on favorite, Junior Caminero (5.3), the home run leader, and Bobby Witt Jr. (6.3) all trail Schlittler’s mark of 7.1. In an award measuring value, Schlittler has statistically impacted his team the most.
The last time a pitcher won MVP was Kershaw in 2014. Spud Chandler also won in 1943, and Guidry finished second in 1978.
The Comparative Case
The American League MVP race at this point is down to five names. Schlittler, Alvarez, Caminero, Witt Jr. and rookie sensation Kevin McGonigle.
Players like Ben Rice and Dillon Dingler were in the thick of the race, but recently played themselves out with .641 and .518 OPS in August, respectively.
Yordan Alvarez
Alvarez is still the favorite, per ESPN. He currently leads baseball in on-base percentage (.427) and slugging percentage (.589), and the American League in batting average (.310). Since his debut in 2019, he has done nothing but mash at the plate, with 2026 his best and healthiest season yet.
It’s hard enough for a primary DH to win MVP. Of course, Ohtani’s done it four of the last five years, but Alvarez isn’t stealing 50 bases or throwing 100 innings. In fact, .
He’s also been abysmal down the stretch. Over the last calendar month (Aug. 15 – Sept. 15) he’s slashed just .238/.375/.393 with two homers and eight RBI. He was once poised to run away with the triple crown, and now it looks like a long shot.
The triple crown is Alvarez’s best bet. If he can turn around these remaining 12 games and reclaim the home run and RBI title, his case is as good as gold. As it stands, Alvarez and Rice are tied for second with 38 home runs to Caminero’s 40. Pete Alonso leads the way with 100 runs driven in, with Alvarez (96) and Caminero (95) close behind.
Junior Caminero
Caminero has been phenomenal in just his 22-year-old season. He’s one of the league’s premier sluggers, hitting 40 homers in 2025 and 2026. He’s a cornerstone on the first-place Tampa Bay Rays.
The main argument against Caminero mirrors Alvarez’s: his game is very one-dimensional. While his hitting prowess is undeniable, he is a negative asset on the base paths and at third base. Unlike Alvarez, he hasn’t cooled off in the final weeks of summer, but at no point this season has he had a narrative driving his MVP case home.
Caminero would surely be a worthy winner. He is a three-true-outcome generator; his batting average sits at a respectable .279.
Bobby Witt Jr.
Then there’s Bobby Witt Jr. He finished second in voting in 2024 and fourth in 2025. He’s perhaps the most well-rounded five -tool player in the league. His game really has no weakness.
2026 could be classified as a “down-year” for him, with “only” a .280 batting average and 18 home runs. He missed about two weeks toward the end of July, so his counting stats aren’t in their usual spot. He doesn’t lead the league in batting, stolen bases, or hits as he has in years past.
He’ll undoubtedly finish towards the top of the ballot, but it’s hard to imagine voters choosing 2026 to reward him. His fifth-place Royals also won’t help his case, especially against the Yankees, Rays and Astros, all currently in a playoff position.
Kevin McGonigle
McGonigle’s rookie season has been excellent. He has split time at shortstop and third base for the Tigers. His offensive profile fits a seasoned veteran. An incredibly balanced slash line of .273/.373/.425 with a nearly even ratio of strikeouts (89) to walks (88). His 6.6 WAR leads position players, but an MLB rookie has only won MVP twice, and not since Ichiro Suzuki in 2001.
It’s hard to imagine a world where McGonigle finds his way atop the voting. Like Witt, he does not lead in any statistical category. His first season in the big leagues has been great, and it’s not far-fetched to say he will take home the award one day, but he will probably finish fifth or sixth in 2026.
Case Closed?
While Aaron Boone endorses his ace as the MVP, teammate and three-time MVP Aaron Judge doesn’t.
“They’ve got a Cy Young Award for a reason, best pitcher in the game. He’s got my vote, definitely, for the Cy Young,” Judge said.
Ultimately, the final two weeks of the season carry a lot of weight. If Yordan Alvarez can turn his bat back on and secure the triple crown, Schlittler stands no chance. If he stays cool and Schlittler has two strong outings left in him, then it might be time to see baseball’s next MVP pitcher.

item.title: [Just Baseball] Cam Schlittler Has Wrapped Up the AL Cy Young Race | Just Baseball
item.dc:creator: Cade Lalim
item.description: Postseason baseball is right around the corner, which means it’s time to analyze a certain starting pitcher who seems to have American League Cy Young honors pretty much wrapped up with a bow. I’m talking about New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler, who’s in the midst of an incredibly successful second season in the majors and looks like he’ll be a force in the league for a long time. After former Detroit Tigers star Tarik Skubal walked away with the American League Cy Young in both 2024 and 2025,
item.content:encoded:
Postseason baseball is right around the corner, which means it’s time to analyze a certain starting pitcher who seems to have American League Cy Young honors pretty much wrapped up with a bow.
I’m talking about New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler, who’s in the midst of an incredibly successful second season in the majors and looks like he’ll be a force in the league for a long time.
After former Detroit Tigers star Tarik Skubal walked away with the American League Cy Young in both 2024 and 2025, Schlittler is looking to assert himself as the new frontline pitcher in the American League. Let’s just say if Skubal didn’t get traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers and still remained on the Detroit Tigers, Schlittler probably still would have the upper hand, which is pretty impressive.
Other elite arms like Dylan Cease, Parker Messick, Drew Rasmussen and Reid Detmers have certainly given him a run for his money, but Schlittler is likely to take home the hardware when it’s all said and done.
He is also looking to be the Yankees’ second Cy Young Award winner in the last four years. Gerrit Cole took home the honors in 2023 after his excellent campaign, in which he owned a 2.63 ERA and 0.98 WHIP. Schlittler’s 2026 campaign has actually been even better.
Now that everything has been set up, it’s time to dig deeper into what has fueled Schlittler’s elite 2026 campaign.
*Stats pulled from games completed through September 14.
Schlittler Came Out of the Blue, Kind Of
Up until the 2025 season, most people probably didn’t even know who Cam Schlittler was and what organization he was a part of. He was drafted by the Yankees in the seventh round of the 2022 draft out of Northeastern University.
He was an all-around solid pitcher in college over his three seasons, posting a 2.62 ERA and 1.08 WHIP, with 30 out of his 31 appearances being starts.
Schlittler didn’t make his affiliated debut within the Yankees system until the 2023 season and showed mixed results between rookie ball, Single-A, and High-A.
Even though he struck out a lot of batters and kept home runs to a minimum, he issued a lot of walks, which inflated his surface numbers.
Over the next two years spanning the 2024 and 2025 seasons, he gradually made his way through the Yankees’ minor league system and started to show some solid improvements.
By the time the 2025 campaign rolled around, Schlittler found himself on MLB Pipeline’s list of the Yankees’ top 30 prospects for the first time, being slotted in at number 12.
He was mowing down hitters, limiting walks, limiting home runs and was simply putting it all together between Double-A and Triple-A.
| Season | HR/9 | BB/9 | K/9 |
| 2023 | 0.8 | 4.1 | 9.8 |
| 2024 | 0.7 | 4.1 | 11.5 |
| 2025 | 0.5 | 3.1 | 11.6 |
Schlittler’s excellent performance was evident to the Yankees front office, and the organization decided it was time to give him a shot at the major league level. Let’s just say it’s been stunning to see what he’s been able to accomplish so quickly.
Pure Dominance in the Majors
Now that I’ve highlighted Schlittler’s underlooked journey to the big leagues, hopefully you’ll appreciate his insane numbers a little more and notice how far he has come along in terms of development.
He had a nice cup of tea with the Yankees in 2025 after he debuted on July 9, finishing the season with an excellent 2.96 ERA and 1.22 WHIP spanning a stretch of 14 starts. A majority of his growth in the minor leagues had carried over to the majors, which was really encouraging to see.
Last year, Schlittler gave us a little glimpse into what he’d provide long term, but no one realized what kind of pitching monster he’d turn into presently in 2026.
You could even argue that he’s been better than Jacob Misiorowski because their numbers have pretty much been identical, give or take. That means you could argue he’s the best pitcher in the majors currently.
So far in 2026, across 31 starts and 184.2 innings pitched, Schlittler has shown pure dominance, pitching to a superb 1.95 ERA and 0.90 WHIP. His ratios have been really good, as backed up by his excellent 6 H/9, 0.8 HR/9, 2.1 BB/9 and 11.1 K/9.
Schlittler currently leads the American League with 5.9 fWAR. He ranks second overall, only trailing Misirowski, who has been worth 6.0 fWAR.
His underlying peripherals look great, including his 2.87 xERA and 2.57 FIP. That is a result of his ability to limit dangerous contact and total baserunners via low hit and walk rates, as previously mentioned.
In terms of pitching run value calculated by Baseball Savant, Schlittler ranks fourth in the majors, currently worth +38 runs. He trails only Yoshinobu Yamamoto (39), Dylan Cease (39) and Jacob Misiorowski (47).
The reason as to why his pitching run value is so high is because of how effective his pitch arsenal has been. Schlittler primarily works with four quality pitches: a four-seam fastball (44%), cutter (25%), sinker (20%) and curveball (10%).
The fastball combo of his four-seam and sinker has been lethal and goes to show how important and effective tunneling can be.
Schlittler’s fastball, which averages 98 mph, is worth a +27 run value, and batters have only managed a .164 batting average and .230 wOBA against the offering. His counterpart 97.8 mph sinker is being valued at a +11 run value, with a .172 batting average and .266 xwOBA.
Also note that Schlittler has 6.8 feet of extension, which places him in the 81st percentile. This helps create a faster perceived velocity for an already powerful fastball mix.
His cutter, which averages 94.7 mph, has been a hint above average with a +1 run value, while his 86.3 mph curveball has been his worst and least-used pitch, worth -1 in run value. If Schlittler can improve just one of those pitches, it could be wraps for his opponents.
Schlittler’s stuff has been very good, to say the least, and batters are having a really hard time making contact on his offerings. His current 34.2% chase rate ranks in the 85th percentile, while his 29.1% whiff rate ranks in the 79th percentile.
Despite the fact that opponents are making limited contact with Schlittler’s offerings, they still have managed to make decent contact when they do connect.
This is one of the few flaws in Schlittler’s already great profile that could use some improvement. Opponents have managed a 7.7% barrel rate (45th percentile) and 39.1% hard-hit (44th percentile) rate against him. Those numbers aren’t bad, but they could be better.
Will Schlittler Take Home AL Cy Young Honors?
Plain and simple, Schlittler has been dominant. And there’s actually a good chance he gets even better down the road based on what we’ve looked at.
It seems very likely that Schlittler will be named the 2026 American League Cy Young when it’s all said and done. Cease has pleaded his case in the best way he’s able to, but all signs are pointing to Schlittler.
Simply just looking at Schlittler’s and Cease’s second-half splits pretty much ends the conversation.
Yordan Alvarez seems like the leading candidate for American League Most Valuable Player, but you’d think Schlittler will be considered there as well. Alvarez leads all AL batters with 5.8 fWAR, but Schlittler does have him topped with 5.9 fWAR — something to keep an eye out for.
We’ll have to wait and see what happens, but Schlittler looks to have wrapped up the conversation for the American League Cy Young.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ pitching picture continues to regain its health, as Clarke Schmidt was reinstated from the 60-day injured list on Wednesday as he returns from Tommy John surgery.
The 30-year-old right-hander had been out since July 3 of last season when he was diagnosed with a torn UCL that not only required Tommy John surgery, but also an internal brace procedure. He had a 3.32 ERA and a 1.090 WHIP in 14 starts last season before the injury
He should be in play for a full-time spot in the rotation next season. Over 30 starts between the 2024 and 2025 seasons, he sported a 3.07 ERA and a 1.140 WHIP, which would make an already-great starting five that much more elite.
In the immediate future, though, Schmidt will likely spend this upcoming postseason in the bullpen. Shortened rotations would likely see the Yankees roll with four starters, and there is no usurping Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, or Carlos Rodon.
To make room for him on the 40-man roster, the Yankees designated utilityman Oswaldo Cabrera for assignment. He played just three games with the big-league club this season, spending most of his time with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre. The 27-year-old was slashing .288/.345/.444 in 122 games, but owned a .635 career OPS across parts of five seasons with the Yankees.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Gerrit Cole Ya No Es Una Elección Segura Ahora Que Los Yankees Se Están Replanteando Su Plan De Pitcheo Para La Postemporada
item.dc:creator: Sara Molnick

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Durante casi toda la última década, a Gerrit Cole le tocaban automáticamente los partidos más importantes de los Yankees.
Esa seguridad se ha esfumado.
A menos de dos semanas de que termine octubre, el lanzador que marcaba la diferencia en el equipo se ha convertido en su mayor incógnita. La velocidad sigue ahí, pero los resultados se han deteriorado en el peor momento posible. Aaron Boone ha intentado restarle importancia a la preocupación. Pero lo que pasa sigue haciendo que eso sea cada vez más difícil.
Cole, ganador del Premio Cy Young de los Yankees en 2023, ha encajado siete jonrones en sus dos últimas salidas, la cifra más alta en cualquier racha de dos salidas de su carrera, según MLB.com. El que antes era una apuesta segura para el primer partido ha bajado puestos en la jerarquía de octubre y ha generado un auténtico debate sobre si debería ser el lanzador titular en un partido a vida o muerte.
Para un equipo de los Yankees que tiene el mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) del béisbol, esto es como una grieta en los cimientos. Nueva York se aseguró el lunes su plaza en los playoffs y ahora tiene un balance de 88-63. El pitcheo es la razón por la que el club cree que puede llegar lejos. Se suponía que Cole iba a ser el pilar de esa fortaleza, no que se convirtiera en su mayor incertidumbre.
Un problema mental que aterroriza a los Yankees
El 6 de septiembre, Cole encajó jonrones de los tres primeros bateadores de los Padres a los que se enfrentó. Fernando Tatis Jr., Jake Cronenworth y Manny Machado conectaron tres jonrones seguidos.
Seis días después, los Mets le dieron una paliza al as de los Yankees en una goleada por 12-2. Francisco Lindor conectó un jonrón con el tercer lanzamiento de Cole. Más tarde, el novato Carson Benge también le mandó la pelota fuera del campo con un slider. Cole aguantó 4 1/3 entradas, encajó cinco carreras y tres jonrones, y se llevó abucheos al salir del campo.
Tras el partido, su explicación hizo que la derrota de los Yankees pareciera aún peor.
Cole tiene una efectividad de 6,08 en sus últimas cuatro salidas, con 17 ponches en 22 2/3 entradas, y ha encajado al menos tres carreras limpias en cuatro partidos seguidos.
En lo que va de temporada, tiene un balance de 8-9, con una efectividad de 3,67 y 20 jonrones permitidos en 115 1/3 entradas. Los Yankees solo han promediado 3,67 carreras en sus salidas, lo que ha convertido partidos que antes parecían pan comido en auténticas loterías.
Lo que realmente preocupa a los Yankees
La preocupación no es que Cole haya perdido de repente su nivel de Grandes Ligas. Es por qué los bateadores se ven tan cómodos frente a él.
Los analistas de YES Network, David Cone y Paul O’Neill, plantearon la posibilidad de que Cole esté delatando sus lanzamientos, lo que podría explicar por qué los bateadores han sabido manejar una bola rápida que sigue alcanzando las 98 mph.
El entrenador de lanzadores, Matt Blake, no lo descartó.
«Es posible», dijo Blake, y añadió que «esa es una de las cosas que vamos a analizar».
Blake también señaló un problema más sencillo. Cole está lanzando strikes a un ritmo sin precedentes en su carrera, pero demasiados se quedan en el centro del strike zone.
«Tenemos que sacar la bola de la parte más ancha del plato», dijo Blake. «Además, quizá tengamos que mejorar la ejecución con dos strikes para lanzar a mejores zonas».
Cole ha reconocido el problema sin pretender haberlo resuelto.
«Hay que empezar a hacer ajustes», dijo Cole.
También rechazó la teoría de que delata sus lanzamientos, diciendo que sus lanzamientos deberían seguir dándonos margen incluso si los bateadores los anticipan.
«Aunque sepan (lo que viene), sigue siendo difícil de batear», dijo Cole. «Mis lanzamientos deberían darnos más margen de error».
Cómo está cambiando la rotación
La mala racha de Cole ha trastocado la jerarquía de la rotación.
Cam Schlittler, en una segunda temporada espectacular, se ha revelado como el mejor lanzador del equipo y un probable candidato al premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana. Se perfila como el abridor del primer partido. Max Fried, que vuelve tras una lesión en el codo, y Carlos Rodón tienen ambos un promedio de carreras limpias por debajo de 3,00 y parecen opciones más seguras para los primeros partidos de la serie.
El enfrentamiento complica aún más las cosas. Es probable que los Yankees se enfrenten a Boston en una serie de comodín al mejor de tres. Cole tiene una efectividad de 5,30 en su carrera contra los Red Sox, y solo los Mets le han bateado con más fuerza.
El veterano columnista Joel Sherman resumió la cuestión de octubre en una sola palabra: «correa». Según su hipótesis, Cole empezaría un partido de mitad de temporada con mucho menos margen de error.
«Creo que Schlittler, Fried y Cole van a ser los titulares», dijo Sherman. «La diferencia es que a Cole le van a dar muy, muy poco margen, algo que, por lo general, no habría tenido».
Sherman también vinculó directamente el techo de los Yankees en la postemporada a que Cole y Aaron Judge recuperen su mejor forma.
«Los Yankees podrían quedarse fuera de los playoffs en menos de 48 horas o podrían ganar la Serie Mundial», dijo Sherman. «Ambas opciones están sobre la mesa y las posibilidades de éxito aumentan mucho más si Cole y Judge se ponen las pilas en las próximas dos semanas, porque son Gerrit Cole y Aaron Judge, y son grandes jugadores cuando están en forma».
Los datos sobre los lanzamientos con efecto explican el colapso
Cole ha mantenido a los bateadores zurdos en un OPS de 0,683. El problema son los bateadores diestros, que tienen un slugging de 0,448 contra él, la cifra más alta que han registrado los diestros en cualquier temporada de su carrera.
Las bolas con efecto del as de los Yankees son las que están causando más daño. Los bateadores diestros tienen un promedio de slugging de 0,652 contra su curva, con diferencia la peor cifra de su carrera. Tienen un promedio de slugging de 0,463 contra su slider, también un récord personal y, con holgada diferencia, su peor marca como jugador de los Yankees.
Además, esos lanzamientos están fallando menos. Su curva solo ha generado un 17 % de fallos contra los bateadores diestros, mientras que su slider se sitúa en el 25 %. Además, está lanzando el slider en el centro de la zona contra los bateadores diestros con la mayor frecuencia de su carrera, lo que explica tanto la reducción de los fallos como los contactos más fuertes.
Los modelos de calidad de los lanzamientos muestran el mismo deterioro. El slider de Cole ha bajado de una puntuación de 125 en Stuff+ en 2020 a 106 esta temporada. La curva de la estrella de los Yankees ha bajado de 120 a 104. Ambas siguen estando por encima de la media, pero el margen que antes le hacía imparable se ha reducido.
Cole cumplió 36 años el 8 de septiembre y está en su primera temporada tras recuperarse de una operación de Tommy John, un año que, según la medicina deportiva, suele ser menos brillante que el segundo. Ya sea por un problema mecánico, por delatar sus lanzamientos o por simple cansancio, Nueva York tiene menos de dos semanas para encontrar la respuesta.
Por ahora, el as que en su día se encargaba de las tareas más importantes está haciendo una prueba para un papel en octubre que antes dominaba.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Cam Schlittler gets poll results that likely ends Cy Young race originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees are currently in the hunt for the AL East and a top Wild Card spot. But that's not the only race going on with the Yankees right now.
Cam Schlittler, the team's ace, is currently vying for the AL Cy Young Award. He has a real chance to win this award, but has to beat out Dylan Cease to head home with some hardware.
Fortunately, a recent poll shared by MLB.com's Jared Greenspan revealed some great news for Schlittler. Out of the 32 voters, all of them named Schlittler as the Cy Young winner.
Cam Schlittler receives 32-out-of-32 votes in Cy Young poll
"1) Cam Schlittler, Yankees (160 total points; 32 first-place votes)," Greenspan shared of MLB.com's 32-expert Cy Young poll.
This poll result should make it clear that Schlittler is the front-runner for the AL Cy Young, if he's not already done enough to secure the award.
The second-year Yankees right-hander has started 31 games, posting a 1.96 ERA with a 14-6 record and 7.0 bWAR with 228 strikeouts in 184.2 innings of work.
While he might not have the 200-plus inning count of some of history's top Cy Young winners, Schlittler has done more than enough to earn this Cy Young award over Cease.
The Yankees' ace has a 216 ERA+, which is the best mark in the American League. Only Jacob Misiorowski can compare to Schlittler overall this season, and the Milwaukee Brewers ace won't challenge Schlittler for this award.
MLB.com's poll results for the AL Cy Young Award revealed that all 32 experts believe Schlittler should win this award. While these aren't the official results, it's a good indicator that Schlittler has a good chance of winning this award.
The 25-year-old ace is looking likely to win the AL Cy Young, as Schlittler's production this season has been nothing short of incredible.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees receive great Clarke Schmidt news amid Twins series originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees already have a strong pitching staff.
Now, they'll be adding another veteran arm with less than two weeks remaining in the regular season.
On Tuesday, Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News reported that right-hander Clarke Schmidt will return from the 60-day injured list on Wednesday.
Schmidt, 30, underwent Tommy John Surgery last July and recently completed a rehab assignment.
He made five appearances between Double-A and Triple-A, throwing one to two innings at a time. According to Anthony Franco of MLB Trade Rumors, Schmidt averaged 94.1 mph on his fastball.
In all likelihood, Schmidt will be an option out of manager Aaron Boone's bullpen, not in the rotation.
New York's rotation already has a more than solid top five of Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodon, and Will Warren.
Schmidt made 14 starts in 2025 before learning surgery was required. He posted a 3.32 ERA and allowed a career-low 6.4 hits per nine innings.
To open space on the active roster, right-hander Bradley Hanner was optioned to Triple-A by the Yankees.

item.title: [New York Post] Every playoff run requires unlikely heroes — and the Yankees’ roster is filled with options
item.dc:creator: Andrew Crane
item.description: When the champagne celebration ended Monday night, after the Yankees removed their goggles and the booze-filled plastic coverings protecting the visitors’ clubhouse at Target Field were taken down, some of their postseason certainties were starting to take shape. Barring a collapse by their own roster, they’ll occupy the
item.content:encoded:
When the champagne celebration ended Monday night, after the Yankees removed their goggles and the booze-filled plastic coverings protecting the visitors’ clubhouse at Target Field were taken down, some of their postseason certainties were starting to take shape.
They, after the Blue Jays lost, had clinched a spot in the tournament. Barring a collapse by the Rays over the final two weeks, the Yankees will start from a wild-card position. Barring a collapse by their own roster, they’ll occupy the top wild-card spot. And barring any last-minute nightmares, Aaron Judge, with his home run Monday as evidence, Max Fried, who’s trying to rediscover his vintage form (as he did in Tuesday’s 8-1 win over the Twins), Gerrit Cole, who’s trying to figure out why he’s letting up all these home runs and Cam Schlittler, in the midst of strengthening his case for the American League Cy Young Award, are all healthy.
But in a year where the Yankees kept needing to navigate injuries, where star after star after star kept missing time, unlikely heroes materialized. And if this group ends up being the one to snap the World Series title drought that dates back to 2009, those names — from Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn to second-half Austin Wells and José Caballero — will need to contribute.
Every contender has its stars. The Judges. The Coles. The Schlittlers, as well as the Frieds, the Ben Rices, the David Bednars and the Cody Bellingers. The constants expected to anchor the run. The faces who’ve been on that October stage before.

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] CC Sabathia Arremete Contra Los Yankees Por El Lío De Volpe Y Lombard Antes De La Inauguración De Su Placa En Monument Park
